0.title: The Kinsman-Redeemer: The Book of Ruth
0.overview:
The book of Ruth is a single perfect pearl set against black velvet. It opens "in the days when the judges ruled" (1:1)—an era the book of Judges sums up with chilling honesty: "everyone did what was right in his own eyes." That period was an age of apostasy, violence, and covenant chaos. And yet here, in the same dark soil, God is quietly cultivating a flower of breathtaking loveliness: a story of loyal love, courageous faith, and redemption that ends, astonishingly, at the cradle of King David and, beyond him, at the manger of David's greater Son. Ruth teaches us that God is never more powerfully at work than when his hand seems most hidden.

At the center of the book stands the Hebrew word hesed—covenant loyalty, steadfast love, grace that keeps its promises when it has no obligation to. It is the word used of God's own faithfulness, and in Ruth it is incarnated in human beings: in Ruth's stunning vow to Naomi, in Boaz's generosity, in the whole shape of the narrative. As Sinclair Ferguson observes, Ruth shows us that hesed is not merely a divine attribute to admire but a way of life into which the redeemed are summoned. The story is, in Tim Keller's memorable phrase, "the gospel in miniature."

The theological heart of the book is the figure of the go'el, the kinsman-redeemer. Under Israelite law, a near relative had the right to redeem a destitute family member—to buy back land, to rescue from slavery, to raise up an heir for a dead kinsman. Boaz becomes the supreme Old Testament type of Christ as Redeemer, because redemption required three things, and he had all three: the right to redeem (he was a kinsman), the resources to redeem (he was wealthy), and—most movingly—the willingness to redeem. He did not have to. He chose to, out of love. In this he prefigures the One who had every right as the eternal Son, who possessed infinite resources in his own precious blood, and who said, "I delight to do your will, O my God."

And there is one more wonder. Ruth is a Moabite—an outsider, a foreigner from a people under covenant curse (Deut 23:3). Yet she is drawn under the wings of the God of Israel by sheer grace, and her name appears in the genealogy of Jesus Christ (Matt 1:5). The gospel reaches the outsider. The barrier between Jew and Gentile, which the cross would one day demolish (Eph 2:11–13), is already being undermined in a barley field outside Bethlehem. Read this book slowly. It is meant to be felt as much as understood—the steadfast love of the LORD shining out of the darkness, and a Redeemer stepping forward who will not let his bride remain empty.

1.title: Emptied and Returning
1.text: <sup>16</sup>But Ruth said, "Do not urge me to leave you or to return from following you. For where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God. <sup>17</sup>Where you die I will die, and there will I be buried. May the LORD do so to me and more also if anything but death parts me from you." (ESV)
1.overview:
Chapter 1 is a chapter of emptying. It opens with famine in Bethlehem—"the house of bread" has no bread—and a family that flees to Moab to survive. There, in a foreign land, the emptying accelerates: Elimelech dies, then both sons die, and Naomi is left a triple widow, stripped of husband, children, and future. The chapter is built on the contrast between fullness and emptiness, and Naomi will name it herself: "I went away full, and the LORD has brought me back empty" (1:21). Here is grief told without flinching, the genuine bitterness of a believer who has been wounded by God's providence and does not pretend otherwise.

Yet against this darkness shines the most luminous human commitment in the Old Testament. At the crossroads, where Orpah turns back—reasonably, understandably—Ruth clings to Naomi and speaks words that have echoed through three millennia: "Where you go I will go... your people shall be my people, and your God my God." Alistair Begg notes that this is not sentiment but covenant; Ruth is binding herself, by oath, to Naomi's people and Naomi's God. A Moabite woman, with no earthly reason for hope, throws in her lot with the covenant community and its God. This is conversion. This is faith. This is grace producing loyalty.

Theologically, the chapter teaches us to read providence with two sets of eyes. Naomi sees only the LORD's heavy hand—and she is not wrong; God is sovereign over her sorrow. But the narrator drops a quiet, electric detail at the chapter's close: they arrived in Bethlehem "at the beginning of barley harvest" (1:22). The reader who knows the rest of the story leans forward. The famine is over. The fields are full. And in those fields, providence is already moving. Naomi feels empty; God is preparing to fill her beyond her dreams.

Keller calls this "the hiddenness of God"—the agonizing season when faith must trust a providence it cannot trace. Romans 8:28 is not yet visible to Naomi, but it is operating in every verse. The God who seems absent is, in fact, never more present than in the wreckage, weaving redemption out of ruin.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — A Family Emptied in Moab
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Famine drives Elimelech and his family from Bethlehem to Moab. There, over a decade, the emptying is total: Elimelech dies, his two sons marry Moabite women, and then both sons die, leaving three childless widows—Naomi, Orpah, and Ruth.
verseByVerse.theology: The opening verses establish the book's governing tension between fullness and emptiness, and they raise the hard question of providence. Was the move to Moab a faithless flight or a desperate necessity? The narrator does not explicitly condemn it, but the relentless dying that follows—three funerals in five verses—casts a shadow. Moab was a place of covenant danger (Num 25; Deut 23:3), and Israel's history with Moab was bitter. Yet God's sovereignty stands over the whole episode; even the deaths that empty Naomi are the dark threads from which God will weave redemption.
verseByVerse.examples: Naomi's family did what families have always done in crisis: they sought survival wherever it could be found, even at the cost of leaving the covenant land and people. Believers in every age face the temptation to solve desperate problems by stepping outside the place of God's blessing. The famine was real; the suffering was real. Ruth refuses to offer cheap answers to the question of why God's people suffer—it simply shows us a family in ruins and dares us to keep reading.

verseByVerse.quote: In the days when the judges ruled there was a famine in the land, and a man of Bethlehem in Judah went to sojourn in the country of Moab, he and his wife and his two sons. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Every word of this opening verse is loaded. "In the days when the judges ruled" places us in the most spiritually chaotic era of Israel's history—the age summarized as "everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (Judg 21:25). It is precisely in that darkness that God will work this jewel of a story; grace shines brightest against the blackest backdrop. Then comes a stinging irony: "a famine in the land," and the man is from "Bethlehem," which means "house of bread." The house of bread has no bread. Wenham and other commentators note that famine in the land of promise is often a covenantal sign, a withdrawal of blessing in response to national sin (Deut 28). The man's response is to "sojourn in the country of Moab." Moab lay east of the Dead Sea, a people descended from Lot's incestuous union (Gen 19) and a perennial enemy of Israel. To flee there was to flee from the place of promise to the place of danger. Yet God's providence is not confined to Bethlehem. As Calvin reminds us, God governs even the wanderings of those who stray, and the wilderness of Moab will become the soil where a Moabite flower of faith will bloom. The story begins in emptiness, but it begins in the hands of God.

verseByVerse.quote: The name of the man was Elimelech and the name of his wife Naomi, and the names of his two sons were Mahlon and Chilion. They were Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah. They went into the country of Moab and remained there. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The names are introduced with the care of a master storyteller, and in Hebrew they speak. "Elimelech" means "My God is King"—a beautiful confession, yet the man bearing it leaves the land where God reigns. "Naomi" means "pleasant" or "sweet," a name she will later renounce in her bitterness (1:20). The sons' names are ominous: "Mahlon" is associated with sickness or weakness, "Chilion" with wasting away or failing. These are not names of vitality; they are names that whisper of the deaths to come. The family are "Ephrathites," an honored clan within Bethlehem—the same Ephrathah of Micah 5:2, from which the Messiah would come. The phrase "remained there" is quietly damning. What was meant to be a temporary sojourn to escape famine becomes a settled life in Moab. Begg observes that this is how compromise so often works—not by a single decisive rebellion, but by a gradual settling into a place we were never meant to stay. The family that left to survive has now put down roots in the land of danger. The narrator offers no comment, only the facts, and lets the unfolding tragedy speak. God's sovereignty, however, is never absent; even here he is preparing a redemption no one can yet see.

verseByVerse.quote: But Elimelech, the husband of Naomi, died, and she was left with her two sons. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The first blow falls, and it falls hard. "Elimelech... died." The man whose name proclaimed "My God is King" is gone, and the narrator's economy of words intensifies the grief rather than diminishing it. Notice the perspective shift: Naomi, not Elimelech, has been the steady reference point, and now the text says "she was left." The verb conveys abandonment, a remnant, a stripping away. In the ancient world, a widow's security lay in her husband and then in her sons; with Elimelech dead, Naomi's survival now hangs on her two frail-named boys, Mahlon and Chilion. Sproul reminds us that the doctrine of providence does not mean God is the author of evil, but it does mean that nothing—not even bereavement in a foreign land—falls outside his sovereign governance. Naomi cannot yet see it, but the God who is King even when his servant has left the land where he reigns is at work in her loss. The emptying has begun. And the reader, who knows the bitterness Naomi will pour out in verse 20, watches with a kind of holy dread, knowing the worst is not yet over. This is grief honestly told, the kind of suffering Scripture never airbrushes, the kind God's people really endure.

verseByVerse.quote: These took Moabite wives; the name of the one was Orpah and the name of the other Ruth. They lived there about ten years, and both Mahlon and Chilion died, so that the woman was left without her two sons and her husband. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The sons marry Moabite women—Orpah and Ruth—and for about ten years there is the appearance of stability. But these were marriages outside the covenant people, with women from a nation under Deuteronomy's solemn warning (Deut 23:3), and the marriages produce no children in a decade. Then the second and third blows fall together with devastating force: "both Mahlon and Chilion died." The crescendo of loss reaches its bottom. The narrator's final clause is almost unbearable in its starkness: "the woman was left without her two sons and her husband." She is not even named here—she is simply "the woman," stripped of every relationship that defined her. In a patriarchal society she is now utterly destitute: no husband to provide, no sons to protect, no grandchildren to carry the family name, no future. Keller observes that Naomi has lost everything that could give a woman of that age security, identity, and hope. The line of Elimelech appears to be extinguished. Humanly speaking, this is a dead end—a family erased from history in a foreign land. And yet God specializes in dead ends. As Carson notes, the God of Scripture characteristically works through human emptiness, weakness, and impossibility, precisely so that the redemption that follows will be unmistakably his doing and his glory.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–18 — The Crossroads: Orpah's Return and Ruth's Vow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hearing that the LORD has visited his people with bread, Naomi sets out to return to Bethlehem. On the road she urges both daughters-in-law to go back to Moab. Orpah, after weeping, returns; but Ruth clings to Naomi and binds herself with an unbreakable oath to Naomi's people and Naomi's God.
verseByVerse.theology: This section turns on the Hebrew word hesed—covenant loyalty, steadfast love that keeps its commitments without obligation. Naomi invokes it as a prayer over her daughters-in-law (v. 8), and Ruth embodies it in her vow. Ruth's confession in vv. 16–17 is one of the great conversions of the Old Testament: a Gentile outsider, with every reason to return to her own gods and people, throws herself entirely upon the God of Israel. This is grace producing faith, and faith producing radical, costly loyalty. It anticipates the gospel's reach to the nations.
verseByVerse.examples: The fork in the road tests every relationship. Orpah's choice is reasonable, even commendable by ordinary standards—she returns to a home and a future. Ruth's choice is extravagant, sacrificial, and risky. Real covenant love is proven not when staying is easy but when leaving would be sensible. Ruth shows us a discipleship that counts the cost and chooses to follow anyway, the kind of all-in commitment Jesus would later require of those who would follow him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then she arose with her daughters-in-law to return from the country of Moab, for she had heard in the fields of Moab that the LORD had visited his people and given them food. So she set out from the place where she was with her two daughters-in-law, and they went on the way to return to the land of Judah. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The first ray of light breaks through. "The LORD had visited his people and given them food." After the long famine, God has acted—and the verb "visited" (paqad) is rich with covenant warmth; it is the word used when God remembers his promises and intervenes in mercy. The famine that opened the book is ending, and Naomi, hearing of it, "arose to return." There is the word that dominates this chapter: return (shub), which appears repeatedly and carries the double sense of physical homecoming and spiritual repentance. Naomi is turning back toward the covenant land she should never have left. Wenham notes that the report comes "in the fields of Moab"—God's mercy to Bethlehem reaches even into the land of exile to draw his people home. Yet notice that the LORD's provision of bread is the thread that begins to pull the whole story toward redemption; the same harvest that feeds Bethlehem will, in chapter 2, bring Ruth to the field of Boaz. Providence is already in motion. Naomi cannot see where this road leads—she sees only the long, sorrowful journey back to a hometown she left full and returns to empty. But God is leading her, and her unlikely companion, straight into the center of his redemptive purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: But Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, "Go, return each of you to her mother's house. May the LORD deal kindly with you, as you have dealt with the dead and with me. The LORD grant that you may find rest, each of you in the house of her husband!" Then she kissed them, and they lifted up their voices and wept. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Naomi's first recorded words are a blessing—and they reveal a heart that, despite its bitterness, still believes in the goodness of the LORD toward others. "May the LORD deal kindly with you"—the word is hesed, that great covenant word for loyal, steadfast love. She prays that God's hesed will reward the hesed her daughters-in-law have shown to the dead and to her. Naomi recognizes that Ruth and Orpah have been faithful, loyal women, and she releases them with grace rather than clinging to them out of need. Her prayer that they "find rest... in the house of her husband" is a prayer for the security of remarriage—the only earthly hope of stability for a widow. There is profound selflessness here: Naomi, desolate herself, urges away the only companions she has left, seeking their good above her own comfort. Ferguson observes that even in her sorrow, Naomi's instinct is to bless and to invoke the covenant love of God—her theology of God's kindness survives her grief. The tears that follow are real; this is the rending of a family forged in shared suffering. Naomi's prayer for "rest" is more prophetic than she knows: God will indeed grant rest, but in a way that will draw at least one of these women not away from Naomi but deeper into the covenant, and into the very line of the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: And they said to her, "No, we will return with you to your people." But Naomi said, "Turn back, my daughters; why will you go with me? Have I yet sons in my womb that they may become your husbands?..." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The daughters-in-law protest their loyalty—"we will return with you to your people"—but Naomi reasons with them, and her argument is rooted in the institution of levirate marriage (Deut 25:5–10), by which a dead man's brother would marry his widow to raise up an heir. Naomi has no more sons; she is too old to bear them; and even if she could, the women could hardly wait. Her logic is airtight, and it is meant to release them from any sense of obligation. But the final clause unveils her heart: "it is exceedingly bitter to me for your sake that the hand of the LORD has gone out against me." Here is the theological crux of Naomi's pain. She does not blame fate or chance or even Moab; she traces her suffering directly to the sovereign hand of the LORD. Sproul notes that this is the honest theology of a true believer—Naomi never doubts God's sovereignty; she only struggles to reconcile it with God's goodness. She is wrong to conclude that the LORD's hand is against her—the reader knows it is secretly for her—but she is right that his hand is in it all. This is the lament of faith: a wounded soul that still addresses its complaint to God, refusing to let go of him even while accusing him. There is more faith in Naomi's bitterness than in many a placid contentment.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they lifted up their voices and wept again. And Orpah kissed her mother-in-law, but Ruth clung to her. And she said, "See, your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and to her gods; return after your sister-in-law." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Here is the great hinge of the chapter, the crossroads where two destinies divide. Both women weep, but their tears flow toward opposite ends. "Orpah kissed her mother-in-law"—a kiss of farewell, the kiss of one who turns back to "her people and to her gods." We should not despise Orpah; her choice is the reasonable one, the one ninety-nine of a hundred would make. She returns to a homeland, a family, a future. But "Ruth clung to her." The verb (dabaq) is the same word used in Genesis 2:24 for a man cleaving to his wife—it speaks of an unbreakable, covenantal joining. Ruth does not merely stay; she fastens herself to Naomi as flesh to flesh. Naomi makes one final attempt to dislodge her, pointing to Orpah as the model: she has gone back "to her people and to her gods"—the phrase exposes the true stakes. To return to Moab is to return to Chemosh and the gods of the nations. To stay with Naomi is to embrace the LORD. Keller draws out the gospel logic here: Orpah chose the sensible, the safe, the calculable; Ruth chose the costly, the risky, the all-in commitment of faith. The kingdom of God is entered not by the cautious but by those who, like Ruth, are willing to lose everything to gain the one thing needful.

verseByVerse.quote: But Ruth said, "Do not urge me to leave you or to return from following you. For where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God. Where you die I will die, and there will I be buried. May the LORD do so to me and more also if anything but death parts me from you." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: These are among the most beautiful words ever spoken by human lips, and they are the spiritual summit of the chapter. Ruth's vow rises in poetic parallels of total surrender: where you go, I go; where you lodge, I lodge; your people, my people; your God, my God; where you die, I die, and there be buried. She binds herself not only to a person but to a people and, supremely, to a God. "Your God my God"—this is the moment of conversion. A Moabite woman, raised on Chemosh, renounces her gods and casts herself wholly upon the LORD, the covenant God of Israel. And she seals it with an oath in the very name of that God: "May the LORD do so to me and more also"—the strongest form of self-imprecation, calling down covenant curses upon herself if she should break faith. Begg notes that Ruth's confession is the more astonishing because she has every earthly reason not to make it: she follows a bitter, empty old woman toward a land of uncertainty, renouncing her own future. This is hesed in its purest human form, and it mirrors the hesed of God himself. Indeed, Ruth's words anticipate the gospel: she is the Gentile outsider drawn by grace into the covenant, the firstfruits of the nations who will one day say of Israel's God, "This God is our God forever and ever." Heaven leans down to hear this vow.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Naomi saw that she was determined to go with her, she said no more. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: A single quiet verse closes the great scene. Naomi, who had argued so strenuously, falls silent. "She said no more." The word translated "determined" suggests Ruth had braced herself, made herself strong, set her face like flint. There is no more arguing with such resolve. This silence is freighted with meaning. It may carry a trace of Naomi's continued numbness—she still cannot see the providence unfolding, and perhaps she even resents the burden of one more mouth to feed in her poverty (a hint of this surfaces in v. 21, where she says she returned "empty," though Ruth stands beside her). Yet the silence also marks acceptance: the bond between these two women is now sealed and unbreakable. Carson observes that the narrator masterfully withholds Naomi's emotional response, letting the reader feel the weight of the moment without resolving it. What Naomi cannot yet grasp is that the very companion she could not dissuade is the instrument God will use to fill her emptiness. The Moabite she sees as another burden is, in the secret purposes of God, the channel of her redemption and the great-grandmother of King David. Ruth's loyalty, which Naomi receives in silence, will prove to be the answer to the prayer Naomi could not even bring herself to pray.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–22 — Empty in Bethlehem, Yet the Harvest Begins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Naomi and Ruth arrive in Bethlehem to a stir of recognition. Naomi pours out her bitterness, renaming herself Mara and declaring that she went out full but the LORD has brought her back empty. Yet the chapter ends with a hinge of hope: they arrive at the beginning of the barley harvest.
verseByVerse.theology: Naomi's lament is a model of honest faith—she attributes everything, even her suffering, to the sovereign hand of the Almighty (Shaddai). She is not faithless; she is wounded, and she brings her wound to God. But her assessment is incomplete: she sees only emptiness where God is preparing fullness. The narrator's closing note—'the beginning of barley harvest'—is the quiet voice of providence, signaling that God's redemptive plan is already in motion even as Naomi despairs.
verseByVerse.examples: Naomi gives believers permission to lament. She does not paper over her pain with pious platitudes; she names her bitterness before God and the community. Yet she is mistaken in reading her circumstances as God's verdict against her. We too judge providence too soon, calling 'empty' what God is about to fill. The barley harvest is a reminder that the seasons of God's mercy often begin precisely when our hope is at its lowest.

verseByVerse.quote: So the two of them went on until they came to Bethlehem. And when they came to Bethlehem, the whole town was stirred because of them. And the women said, "Is this Naomi?" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The journey ends; the two women reach Bethlehem, and the whole town is "stirred"—the Hebrew suggests a buzzing commotion, a ripple of astonishment running through the community. "Is this Naomi?" The question is pregnant with shock. The woman who left perhaps a decade ago—wife, mother of two sons, part of a prosperous Ephrathite family—returns gaunt with grief, aged by sorrow, accompanied only by a Moabite widow. The years and the losses are written on her face. There is something deeply human in this scene: the small town that remembers, the recognition that is half-disbelief, the way suffering can transform a person until old neighbors scarcely know her. Wenham notes the literary artistry—the repetition of "came to Bethlehem" slows the narrative, letting us feel the weight of homecoming. And there is irony in the place itself: Naomi returns to "the house of bread" empty-handed, just as the bread is returning to the house (the harvest is beginning). The community's astonished question sets up Naomi's bitter reply. She is about to reinterpret her very identity in light of her suffering. But the reader, standing at the threshold of the harvest, senses what Naomi cannot—that this homecoming, which looks like the end of a tragedy, is in fact the opening of redemption's great work.

verseByVerse.quote: She said to them, "Do not call me Naomi; call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me. I went away full, and the LORD has brought me back empty. Why call me Naomi, when the LORD has testified against me and the Almighty has brought calamity upon me?" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Here is the emotional and theological heart of the chapter—Naomi's great lament. She rejects her own name: "Do not call me Naomi" (pleasant); "call me Mara" (bitter), "for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me." Four times in two verses she names God as the author of her affliction—Shaddai (the Almighty) twice, and the LORD (Yahweh) twice. This is no atheist's complaint; it is the lament of a robust believer who knows that nothing happens outside the sovereign hand of God. "I went away full, and the LORD has brought me back empty." Sproul observes that Naomi's theology is more orthodox than that of many comfortable Christians—she never imagines God is absent or powerless; she traces every loss to his hand. Yet her conclusion is profoundly mistaken: she reads her emptiness as God's verdict against her ("the LORD has testified against me"). And here lies the deep irony the narrator wants us to feel: Naomi says she returned "empty," but Ruth—loyal, faithful, soon to be the mother of the line of David—is standing right beside her. The vessel of her future fullness is the very person she does not even count. Keller draws the lesson: we are terrible judges of our own circumstances, declaring "empty" what God has filled, calling "bitter" the providence that is sweet beyond our imagining. Naomi's lament is honest, and God can bear it; but it is not the last word.

verseByVerse.quote: So Naomi returned, and Ruth the Moabite her daughter-in-law with her, who returned from the country of Moab. And they came to Bethlehem at the beginning of barley harvest. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter closes with a verse that seems merely to summarize but in fact turns the whole story toward hope. The narrator pointedly calls Ruth "the Moabite"—a reminder of her outsider status that will be repeated through the book, making her inclusion all the more astonishing. And he notes that she "returned from the country of Moab," though Ruth had never been to Bethlehem; her "return" is the return of faith, the homecoming of a soul to the people and God of the covenant. Then comes the hinge: "they came to Bethlehem at the beginning of barley harvest." This is the quiet voice of providence, and the alert reader's pulse quickens. The barley harvest fell in spring (around April), the season of new beginnings, of bread returning to the house of bread. Just as Naomi declares herself empty, the fields of Bethlehem are filling with grain. And it is into those very fields that Ruth will go to glean in chapter 2—the fields of a man named Boaz. Carson notes the narrator's exquisite timing: every detail is set, the stage is prepared, the harvest of redemption is about to begin. Naomi sees only emptiness; God has scheduled the harvest. The chapter of emptying ends with the first sheaf of fullness ripening in the sun.

1.theology:
The Sovereignty of God in Suffering. Chapter 1 presents a robust, unflinching doctrine of providence. Naomi traces every loss—famine, bereavement, emptiness—directly to the hand of the LORD and the Almighty (vv. 13, 20–21). The book never suggests God is absent from the tragedy; rather, he governs it. Yet Naomi's error is to conclude that God's sovereign hand in her suffering means God's heart is against her. The narrator quietly corrects this by the closing note of harvest. Romans 8:28 operates in this chapter long before Naomi can perceive it: the God who empties is the God who is preparing to fill, and his hidden providence is working all things—even the deaths in Moab—toward a redemption that will reach to the manger of Bethlehem.

Hesed: Steadfast Covenant Love. The Hebrew word hesed—loyal, faithful, unbreakable love—pulses through the chapter. Naomi prays for it over her daughters-in-law (v. 8); Ruth embodies it in her vow (vv. 16–17). It is the word used of God's own covenant faithfulness, and here it becomes incarnate in human commitment. Ruth's hesed toward Naomi mirrors and points to the hesed of God toward his people—a love that keeps its promises when it has no obligation to do so.

The Conversion of the Outsider. Ruth's confession, "your God my God," is one of the great conversions of the Old Testament. A Moabite, from a people under covenant curse, casts herself wholly on the LORD by sheer grace. She is the firstfruits of the Gentile inclusion, the foreshadowing of the gospel reaching the nations—the dividing wall already cracking in a barley field outside Bethlehem.
1.examples:
Then: In the ancient world, a widow without husband or sons was among the most vulnerable people in society—economically destitute, socially marginal, without legal standing or future. Naomi's despair was not exaggerated; it reflected the brutal realities of her time. Ruth's decision to follow her meant binding herself to that same vulnerability, choosing poverty and uncertainty in a foreign land over the security of her homeland. Her loyalty was costly in the most concrete terms.

Now: Naomi gives believers today permission to lament honestly. She does not mask her pain with forced cheerfulness; she names her bitterness before God and the community. Yet she also warns us against reading our circumstances as God's final verdict. How often we declare a season 'empty' that God is about to fill, or call 'bitter' a providence whose sweetness we cannot yet taste. Ruth, meanwhile, models the all-in commitment of faith—choosing the costly path of loyal love over the sensible path of self-protection. In an age that prizes keeping our options open, Ruth's unconditional 'where you go I will go' confronts us with the radical, covenantal nature of true discipleship.

2.title: Under His Wings
2.text: <sup>12</sup>The LORD repay you for what you have done, and a full reward be given you by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge! (ESV)
2.overview:
Chapter 2 moves from the dark interiors of grief into the open fields under the spring sun, and the whole atmosphere lifts. Ruth, the destitute foreigner, goes out to glean—to exercise the right of the poor under Israel's law (Lev 19:9–10; Deut 24:19–22) to gather the grain left at the edges and corners of the fields. It is hard, humbling, hand-to-mouth labor, the work of survival. And yet into this ordinary scene God weaves an extraordinary providence. "She happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz" (2:3)—and that little phrase, which seems to speak of chance, is the narrator's gentle joke, for the reader knows there are no accidents in the economy of God.

Boaz is introduced as "a worthy man" (2:1)—a man of substance, standing, and integrity—and he is a relative of Elimelech. When he arrives in his field, his very first words are a benediction: "The LORD be with you" (2:4). Here is a man whose faith permeates his work and his speech. His treatment of Ruth becomes the moving center of the chapter. He protects her, provides for her, eats with her, and deliberately commands his workers to leave extra grain for her to find. He goes far beyond the requirements of the law; the gleaning legislation set a floor, but Boaz's grace knows no ceiling. As Keller observes, the law established the minimum; Boaz's generosity reveals the heart of God, which always gives more than is required.

The theological jewel of the chapter is Boaz's blessing in verse 12: "a full reward be given you by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge." The image of taking refuge under the wings (kanaf) of the LORD is one of the tenderest pictures of God in all of Scripture—the great Almighty as a mother bird sheltering her young. Ruth has fled to the God of Israel for refuge, and Boaz prays that God will reward her. He does not yet know that he himself will become the answer to his own prayer—that in chapter 3 Ruth will ask him to spread his own "wings" (the same Hebrew word) over her. The man who prays for God's protective wings will become the human means by which those wings are spread.

Above all, this chapter teaches us how God's providence ordinarily works—not usually through dramatic miracles, but through the faithful, generous obedience of ordinary people and the quiet orchestration of "coincidence." Ferguson notes that the hidden God of chapter 1 is the providing God of chapter 2, and his provision comes through human kindness. Behind Boaz's open hand is the open hand of God; under Boaz's protective care, Ruth is being drawn under the wings of the Almighty.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Ruth Goes Out to Glean
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Boaz is introduced as a worthy relative of Elimelech. Ruth, taking initiative, asks to glean in the fields, and 'happens' to come to the portion belonging to Boaz. The narrator's understated 'happened' is the chapter's great irony: in God's world, there are no accidents.
verseByVerse.theology: These verses introduce the doctrine of providence as the book's engine. The Hebrew phrase translated 'she happened to come' (literally 'her chance chanced upon') is deliberately ironic. The narrator uses the language of coincidence precisely to make the reader smile, knowing that what looks like luck is the orchestration of a sovereign God. Boaz is introduced as a 'worthy man'—the same Hebrew root (gibbor hayil) used of valiant warriors—signaling that he is a man of substance and integrity who will play a decisive role.
verseByVerse.examples: Ruth does not sit passively waiting for provision; she takes initiative, going out to do hard, humble labor. Yet her diligence and God's providence are not in competition—she works, and God guides her steps. Believers are called to the same: to labor faithfully in the ordinary while trusting that God governs the 'chances' that shape our lives. The intersection of human responsibility and divine sovereignty is not a problem to solve but a partnership to live.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Naomi had a relative of her husband's, a worthy man of the clan of Elimelech, whose name was Boaz. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: With the deftness of a master narrator, the writer steps aside from the action to plant a seed of hope in the reader's mind before either Naomi or Ruth knows of it. "Naomi had a relative of her husband's"—the Hebrew word (moda) suggests a known kinsman, and crucially he is "of the clan of Elimelech." The careful reader, remembering the laws of kinship and redemption, immediately senses possibility: a near relative could redeem. He is described as "a worthy man"—the phrase is gibbor hayil, the very term used of mighty warriors and men of valor (it describes Gideon and Boaz alike), but here it denotes a man of wealth, standing, and sterling character. And his name is given at last: "Boaz," which may mean "in him is strength." The name will prove fitting; he will be the strong redeemer the story needs. Wenham observes the artistry: the narrator introduces Boaz to us, the readers, while leaving the characters in the dark, so that we watch the unfolding providence with eyes they do not yet have. We know the redeemer is in place before Ruth ever sets foot in his field. This is how the narrator teaches us to read providence—God has already positioned the answer before the need is felt. Boaz is on the stage; the gospel of redemption is about to be enacted in a barley field, and the strong, worthy man at the center of it points beyond himself to the Redeemer who is strength and worth itself.

verseByVerse.quote: And Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi, "Let me go to the field and glean among the ears of grain after him in whose sight I shall find favor." And she said to her, "Go, my daughter." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Again the narrator calls her "Ruth the Moabite"—the label of the outsider, repeated to keep her foreignness before us, so that the grace shown to her will land with full force. And it is Ruth, not Naomi, who takes the initiative. Naomi remains passive in her grief; it is the young foreign widow who proposes to go out and work. Gleaning was the provision Israel's law made for the poor, the widow, the orphan, and the sojourner (Lev 19:9–10; Deut 24:19–22): landowners were forbidden to harvest the corners of their fields or to gather what was dropped, leaving it for the destitute to gather by hand. It was honest but humble labor, and not without danger for a vulnerable foreign woman in the fields. Ruth's words are telling: she hopes to glean "after him in whose sight I shall find favor." The word "favor" (hen) is the language of grace—undeserved kindness. Ruth knows she has no claim; she can only hope to find grace. Begg notes that Ruth's faith expresses itself in diligent, humble work joined to hope in God's kindness through others. She does not presume; she labors and trusts. Naomi's simple reply, "Go, my daughter," is the first warm word she has spoken since her bitter lament—a small thaw in the ice of her grief. The stage is set; the destitute Moabite goes out to glean, and providence goes out with her.

verseByVerse.quote: So she set out and went and gleaned in the field after the reapers, and she happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz, who was of the clan of Elimelech. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is one of the most theologically loaded verses in all of Scripture, and its power lies in its deliberate understatement. "She happened to come"—the Hebrew is even more striking, literally "her chance chanced upon" the field of Boaz. The narrator uses the language of pure coincidence, of random luck, and he does so with a twinkle in his eye. For the reader has just been told in verse 1 that Boaz is a worthy kinsman of Elimelech—and now Ruth "just happens" to wander into his field, out of all the fields around Bethlehem. Sproul calls this the great irony of the book: the narrator describes the most providentially orchestrated event in the entire story using the language of accident, precisely to teach us that in God's universe there is no such thing as chance. What looks like luck to us is the fingerprint of a sovereign God who governs every footstep. Calvin's doctrine of providence finds perfect illustration here: God's hand is not less present in the ordinary and the apparently random than in the spectacular miracle; indeed, it is most often through these unremarked 'coincidences' that he accomplishes his greatest purposes. Ruth thinks she is making an arbitrary choice of field; God is leading her by the hand to her redeemer. Keller draws the lesson: the events we call accidents and coincidences are the unobserved providence of God, weaving the pattern of our lives toward ends we cannot see. There are no random fields in the kingdom of God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Boaz arrives and greets his workers with a blessing. Noticing Ruth, he learns who she is and showers her with extraordinary kindness—protection, water, a noonday meal, and deliberate provision of extra grain. He blesses her for her loyalty to Naomi and prays that the God under whose wings she has taken refuge will fully reward her.
verseByVerse.theology: Boaz embodies grace that goes beyond law. The gleaning laws set a minimum standard of provision for the poor; Boaz vastly exceeds it, commanding his workers to pull out extra grain on purpose (v. 16). This is the heart of the gospel pattern: the law establishes a floor, but grace knows no ceiling. Boaz's famous blessing in v. 12—'under whose wings you have come to take refuge'—presents one of Scripture's tenderest images of God as a sheltering refuge, an image Jesus himself would take up over Jerusalem (Matt 23:37).
verseByVerse.examples: Boaz models faith that saturates daily work. His first words to his laborers are a benediction; he treats a destitute foreign woman with dignity, generosity, and protection. He shows us what it looks like when piety is not confined to the temple but overflows into the marketplace, the field, and the treatment of the vulnerable. The hidden providence of God so often comes to others through the open hands of his obedient people.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, Boaz came from Bethlehem. And he said to the reapers, "The LORD be with you!" And they answered, "The LORD bless you." Then Boaz said to his young man who was in charge of the reapers, "Whose young woman is this?" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The narrator's "And behold" invites us to look up: at the precise moment Ruth is gleaning, Boaz himself "came from Bethlehem" into his field. The timing is, of course, no accident—it is the same providence that brought Ruth to this field that now brings the field's owner to her. And what are the first words out of Boaz's mouth? "The LORD be with you!"—a benediction upon his workers. And they answer in kind: "The LORD bless you." This brief exchange tells us everything about the spiritual climate of Boaz's household. Here, in the dark days of the judges when "everyone did what was right in his own eyes," is a man whose faith flows naturally into his speech and his relationships with his laborers. His piety is not Sabbath-only; it permeates the workplace. Ferguson observes that Boaz is the kind of man whose godliness is most visible precisely where godliness is hardest to sustain—in the rough, transactional world of business and labor. Then Boaz notices the newcomer: "Whose young woman is this?" In that culture a woman belonged to a household; Boaz's question is the proper inquiry of a responsible man. It is also the question that opens the door to everything that follows. The redeemer has entered his field, blessing in his mouth, and has caught sight of the woman he will redeem. The reader, who knows the kinship, can scarcely breathe.

verseByVerse.quote: And the servant who was in charge of the reapers answered, "She is the young Moabite woman, who came back with Naomi from the country of Moab. She said, 'Please let me glean and gather among the sheaves after the reapers.' So she came, and she has continued from early morning until now, except for a short rest." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The foreman's report is rich with detail and, again, marks Ruth as "the young Moabite woman"—the outsider label that the narrator and now the characters keep pressing, so that the grace about to be shown will be all the more striking. The foreman testifies to two things. First, Ruth's humility: she did not presume upon any right but "asked"—"Please let me glean"—she sought permission and gleaned only "after the reapers," taking the lowest place, claiming nothing. Second, her diligence: she "has continued from early morning until now, except for a short rest." This is a woman of remarkable industry, laboring tirelessly in the hot field for the bare survival of herself and Naomi. The foreman's unprompted commendation functions as a character witness; Ruth's reputation as a hard worker has already preceded any kindness from Boaz. Wenham notes that the narrator is building our admiration for Ruth before Boaz's generosity descends, so that we feel her worthiness and her need together. There is also a quiet theology of work here: Ruth's faith is not passive. She trusts God, and she labors from dawn. Her industry does not earn the grace that is coming, but it is the seedbed in which God's providence will be sown. The diligent foreigner has caught the attention not only of Boaz but, the reader senses, of the God who notices the labor of the lowly and the cry of the widow and the stranger.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Boaz said to Ruth, "Now, listen, my daughter, do not go to glean in another field or leave this one, but keep close to my young women. Let your eyes be on the field that they are reaping, and go after them. Have I not charged the young men not to touch you? And when you are thirsty, go to the vessels and drink what the young men have drawn." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Boaz's first words to Ruth are tender and protective: "my daughter." Though they will later marry, here he speaks as a guardian, putting the vulnerable foreigner at ease. And his kindness is immediate and concrete. He invites her to stay in his field—not to wander to others where she might be exposed to danger or hostility—and to glean alongside his own young women, under the umbrella of his household's protection. Then comes a striking detail: "Have I not charged the young men not to touch you?" The word implies protection from harassment or assault. A young foreign widow gleaning alone was tragically vulnerable; Boaz has explicitly forbidden his male workers from molesting her. Finally, he offers her free access to the water his men have drawn—a reversal of the social order, for normally the foreigner would draw water for the Israelites, but here the Israelite provides for the foreigner. Keller notes that Boaz's protection prefigures the way Christ shelters his own: he does not merely permit the vulnerable to come near; he actively guards them, removing every threat, providing for every need. Already, before any romance, Boaz is functioning as a kind of redeemer—covering, protecting, providing. The wings of refuge he will pray for in verse 12 are, in these very commands, beginning to spread over Ruth. Grace is not waiting; it is already at work through the open hand of a godly man.

verseByVerse.quote: Then she fell on her face, bowing to the ground, and said to him, "Why have I found favor in your eyes, that you should take notice of me, since I am a foreigner?" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Ruth's response is one of the most beautiful expressions of grace-astonishment in Scripture. She "fell on her face, bowing to the ground"—a posture of profound humility and gratitude. And her question pierces to the heart of the gospel: "Why have I found favor in your eyes... since I am a foreigner?" The word "favor" is hen—grace, unmerited kindness—and the word "foreigner" (nokriyah) emphasizes her complete lack of any claim. She is an alien, an outsider, a Moabite from a cursed people; she has done nothing to deserve Boaz's attention. Her question is the question every recipient of grace must ask: Why me? Why should I, who have no right, be shown such kindness? Begg observes that Ruth's wonder at being "noticed" is the very wonder of the redeemed soul before the grace of God. The believer never gets over the question "Why have I found favor in your eyes?" There is a deliberate wordplay in the Hebrew here that the English cannot fully capture: "take notice" (nakar) and "foreigner" (nokriyah) share a root, so Ruth is essentially saying, "Why have you 'recognized' me, an 'unrecognizable' one?" The very thing that should have made her invisible—her foreignness—has become the occasion for grace. This is the scandal and glory of the gospel: God notices precisely those who have no claim, and the outsider becomes the object of redeeming love.

verseByVerse.quote: But Boaz answered her, "All that you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband has been fully told to me, and how you left your father and mother and your native land and came to a people that you did not know before." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Boaz answers Ruth's bewildered question by revealing that her reputation has preceded her: "All that you have done... has been fully told to me." The grace she could not understand is, in part, a response to the hesed she had shown. Boaz recounts it: she stood by Naomi after her husband's death; she "left your father and mother and your native land" and came "to a people that you did not know." The careful reader hears an unmistakable echo. This is the language of Genesis 12:1, where God called Abraham to leave "your country and your kindred and your father's house" and go to a land he did not know. Wenham and others note this deliberate allusion: Ruth, the Moabite outsider, has made an Abraham-like journey of faith. She has left everything and ventured into the unknown, trusting the God of Israel. She is, in effect, a daughter of Abraham by faith, even though she is not his daughter by blood—exactly the principle Paul would later expound (Gal 3:7, "it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham"). Boaz sees in this foreign woman the marks of true faith and self-giving loyalty, and he honors them. Yet we must not mistake the order: Ruth's loyalty does not earn the redemption to come; rather, it is the fruit of the faith that has already taken hold of her. The grace that drew her to the God of Israel now flowers in the very love that Boaz commends.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD repay you for what you have done, and a full reward be given you by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is the theological summit of the chapter, and one of the tenderest verses in all of Scripture. Boaz pronounces a benediction: "The LORD repay you... a full reward... under whose wings you have come to take refuge." The image is breathtaking. The Hebrew word for "wings" is kanaf—the wing of a bird—and it pictures the Almighty God of Israel as a mother bird sheltering her young beneath her feathers. Ruth, the homeless Moabite widow, has not merely come to Bethlehem; she has come to take refuge under the wings of the LORD. This is the very heart of saving faith: fleeing to God as one's shelter, hiding beneath the covering of his protective love. The image runs like a golden thread through Scripture—"in the shadow of your wings I will take refuge" (Ps 57:1); "he will cover you with his pinions, and under his wings you will find refuge" (Ps 91:4)—and it reaches its most poignant expression on the lips of Jesus weeping over Jerusalem: "How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!" (Matt 23:37). But here is the wonder Boaz cannot yet see: in chapter 3, Ruth will ask him to spread his own "wings" (the same word, kanaf) over her—to become her redeemer. The man who prays that God's wings would shelter Ruth will himself become the human means by which those wings are spread. Boaz prays a prayer he will answer with his own life.

verseByVerse.quote: Then she said, "I have found favor in your eyes, my lord, for you have comforted me and spoken kindly to your servant, though I am not one of your servants." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Ruth receives Boaz's blessing with grateful wonder, and her words again breathe the spirit of grace. "I have found favor in your eyes"—she names the grace (hen) she had questioned in verse 10, now received and embraced. "You have comforted me"—the word speaks of consolation to one in grief, and it is striking, for Ruth and Naomi had returned in such sorrow; here at last is comfort. "You have spoken kindly to your servant"—literally, "you have spoken to the heart" of your servant, an idiom for words of tenderness and reassurance. And then the crowning humility: "though I am not one of your servants." Ruth recognizes that she has no standing in Boaz's household; she is not even among his hired women. She has no claim on his kindness whatsoever, and so his grace astonishes her all the more. Ferguson notes that this is the perpetual posture of the redeemed: never presuming, never taking grace for granted, always marveling that such kindness should be shown to one with no claim. There is a profound dignity-in-humility here; Ruth does not grovel, but neither does she presume. She simply receives, with open and grateful hands, what she has not earned. Boaz's kind words have done what no mere provision of grain could do—they have comforted a grieving heart and made an outsider feel, for the first time since her losses, that she has found a place of welcome. This is the comfort of the gospel in miniature: to be spoken to tenderly by the one who has every right to ignore us.

verseByVerse.quote: And at mealtime Boaz said to her, "Come here and eat some bread and dip your morsel in the wine." So she sat beside the reapers, and he passed to her roasted grain. And she ate until she was satisfied, and she had some left over. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Boaz's kindness now becomes table fellowship—and in the ancient world, to share a meal was to share community, to extend belonging. "Come here and eat... dip your morsel in the wine." Boaz invites the foreign gleaner to eat with his own reapers, dissolving the social barrier between the destitute outsider and the harvesters of the field. "So she sat beside the reapers"—Ruth, the Moabite widow, is given a place at the table. And then "he passed to her roasted grain"—Boaz himself, the master of the field, serves her with his own hand. The detail is exquisite: such personal attention to a nobody. The verse ends with quiet abundance: "she ate until she was satisfied, and she had some left over." The word "satisfied" speaks of fullness, of being filled to the point of having more than enough—a striking reversal for the woman who came from a household defined by emptiness and famine. Keller draws out the gospel resonance: here is a foreigner welcomed to the table, served by the lord of the harvest, filled to overflowing with provision she could never have earned. It is a foretaste of the great supper of the Lamb, where outsiders from every nation are gathered to a table they had no right to, served by the Lord himself, and satisfied forever. The leftover grain she will carry home to Naomi—provision so abundant it spills beyond the recipient to bless another. Grace, when it comes, comes in baskets that overflow.

verseByVerse.quote: When she rose to glean, Boaz instructed his young men, saying, "Let her glean even among the sheaves, and do not reproach her. And also pull out some from the bundles for her and leave it for her to glean, and do not rebuke her." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Here Boaz's grace soars past every legal requirement, and the narrator lets us listen in on the private instructions he gives his workers—instructions Ruth herself does not hear. The gleaning law permitted the poor to gather only from the corners and what was dropped (Lev 19:9–10); but Boaz commands his men to let Ruth "glean even among the sheaves"—in the heart of the harvest, where gleaners were never normally allowed. More than that: "pull out some from the bundles for her and leave it"—deliberately drop extra grain, on purpose, where she will find it, so that her gathering will be rich. And twice he charges them not to "reproach" or "rebuke" her. This is the very heart of the chapter's theology. The law set a floor for provision; Boaz's grace knows no ceiling. He does not give Ruth the minimum the law requires; he lavishes upon her far more than she could ever deserve or expect, and he does it secretly, so that she experiences it simply as the bounty of the field. Keller's insight is unforgettable here: this is precisely how the grace of God works. God does not deal with us according to the strict requirements of the law; he engineers our circumstances so that grace overflows where we least expect it, leaving "handfuls on purpose" for us to find. Behind every unexpected provision, every undeserved kindness that meets us, is a Redeemer who has secretly instructed the circumstances of our lives to bless us beyond all law and merit.

verseByVerse.quote: So she gleaned in the field until evening. Then she beat out what she had gleaned, and it was about an ephah of barley. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The day's labor closes with a striking measure of its fruit. Ruth gleaned "until evening"—from early morning (v. 7) to dusk, a full day of relentless work—and when she "beat out what she had gleaned," the yield was "about an ephah of barley." An ephah was a substantial quantity, somewhere around thirty pounds of grain, an amount that would feed Ruth and Naomi for many days, perhaps weeks. For an ordinary gleaner, such a harvest in a single day would have been extraordinary—it is the visible result of Boaz's secret generosity, the "handfuls on purpose" now weighed out in the basket. The narrator lets the abundance speak. Ruth set out hoping merely to survive, to glean enough to keep two widows alive; she returns staggering under a harvest of plenty. Wenham notes the deliberate contrast with chapter 1: the woman associated with a household of emptiness now carries home overflowing abundance. The God who emptied Naomi (1:21) is beginning, through the kindness of Boaz, to fill her again. And the means is so ordinary: a day's honest labor in a barley field, blessed beyond measure by hidden grace. There is a quiet sermon in this ephah of barley—that the God of providence often pours out his most lavish gifts through the most mundane channels, and that the diligent hand of faith, joined to the secret generosity of grace, comes home full. Ruth's basket is heavy with more than grain; it is heavy with the dawning of redemption.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ruth brings the abundant grain home, and Naomi's astonishment leads to the revelation that the man who showed such kindness is Boaz, 'one of our redeemers.' For the first time, Naomi blesses the LORD and her bitterness begins to thaw. Ruth continues gleaning through the barley and wheat harvests.
verseByVerse.theology: The key word emerges: go'el, kinsman-redeemer. Naomi recognizes that Boaz is 'a close relative... one of our redeemers' (v. 20), and for the first time since her lament she blesses the LORD, declaring that his hesed has not forsaken the living or the dead. The hidden providence of chapter 1 is becoming visible; the empty woman dares to hope again. The concept of the go'el—a near kinsman with the right and duty to redeem—is the theological key to the entire book and the central type of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Naomi's transformation models how the perception of God's kindness revives a grieving heart. The same woman who said the Almighty had dealt bitterly with her now blesses the LORD whose kindness has not forsaken her. Often it is the tangible evidence of God's providential care—through the kindness of others—that begins to heal our bitterness and rekindle hope. God's mercies, once perceived, melt the ice of despair.

verseByVerse.quote: And she took it up and went into the city. Her mother-in-law saw what she had gleaned. She also brought out and gave her what food she had left over after being satisfied. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Ruth carries the heavy ephah of barley back into the city, and Naomi "saw what she had gleaned." We can imagine the astonishment on the old woman's face—such an enormous quantity from a single day's gleaning could only mean that something remarkable had happened in the field. But before Naomi can even ask, Ruth does something that reveals her character once more: "she also brought out and gave her what food she had left over after being satisfied." Remember verse 14—Ruth had eaten until she was full and had food left over. And what did she do with the leftover? She did not consume it herself or hoard it; she carried it home to share with Naomi. This small detail is a window into Ruth's selfless love. Even the abundance she received at Boaz's table becomes provision for the mother-in-law she has vowed to serve. Begg notes that genuine grace received always overflows in grace given; the one who has been filled cannot help but share. Ruth's hesed toward Naomi continues unabated—she labors all day, eats sparingly enough to save some, and brings the surplus home. The destitute foreigner is feeding the Israelite widow, the very reversal that has marked this entire chapter. And Naomi, who declared herself "empty" in chapter 1, now sees with her own eyes the evidence of returning fullness, carried through her door by the loyal hands of the daughter-in-law she once tried to send away.

verseByVerse.quote: And her mother-in-law said to her, "Where did you glean today? And where have you worked? Blessed be the man who took notice of you." So she told her mother-in-law with whom she had worked, saying, "The man's name with whom I worked today is Boaz." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The sheer abundance prompts Naomi's eager questions: "Where did you glean today? And where have you worked?" And before she even learns the name, she pronounces a blessing: "Blessed be the man who took notice of you." The word "took notice" (nakar) is the same root used in verse 10 when Ruth marveled that Boaz should notice a "foreigner." Naomi instinctively recognizes that such a harvest could only come from extraordinary kindness, and she blesses the unknown benefactor. Then comes the dramatic revelation, delivered by the narrator with careful timing for maximum effect: "The man's name with whom I worked today is Boaz." The reader, of course, has known since verse 1 that Boaz is a kinsman of Elimelech, and has been waiting for this moment of recognition. Now Naomi learns it, and her response in the next verse will show that she grasps its full significance. Wenham notes the narrator's skill in withholding and then releasing information; the name "Boaz" lands like a thunderclap of providence. What Ruth experienced merely as the kindness of a generous stranger, Naomi will immediately recognize as the hand of God orchestrating redemption. The "chance" of verse 3 is about to be unmasked as the design of God. The man Ruth happened upon is precisely the man positioned by heaven to redeem them. Hope, long dead in Naomi's heart, is about to draw its first breath.

verseByVerse.quote: And Naomi said to her daughter-in-law, "May he be blessed by the LORD, whose kindness has not forsaken the living or the dead!" Naomi also said to her, "The man is a close relative of ours, one of our redeemers." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This verse marks the turning of Naomi's soul. For the first time since her bitter lament in chapter 1, Naomi blesses the LORD—and notice the radical shift. In 1:20–21 she said the Almighty had dealt bitterly with her and that the LORD had brought her back empty; now she cries, "May he be blessed by the LORD, whose kindness has not forsaken the living or the dead!" The word for "kindness" is hesed—that great covenant word for steadfast, loyal love. The same woman who felt abandoned by God now perceives that his hesed has never let go of her family, whether "the living" (herself and Ruth) or "the dead" (Elimelech and her sons, whose line may yet be preserved). The ice of bitterness is melting under the warmth of perceived grace. And then the pivotal word of the entire book is spoken: Boaz is "one of our redeemers." The Hebrew is go'el—the kinsman-redeemer. Under Israel's law, the go'el was a near relative who bore the right and the responsibility to rescue a family member in distress: to buy back land sold in poverty (Lev 25:25), to redeem a relative sold into slavery (Lev 25:47–49), to avenge a slain kinsman (Num 35:19), and, by extension, to marry a childless widow and raise up an heir for the dead. Sproul observes that the go'el is the great Old Testament type of Christ, who is our near kinsman by the incarnation, and who has the right, the resources, and the willingness to redeem his people. Naomi sees it: in Boaz, God has provided a redeemer. The empty woman has been given a future.

verseByVerse.quote: And Ruth the Moabite said, "Besides, he said to me, 'You shall keep close by my young men until they have finished all my harvest.'" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Once more the narrator labels her "Ruth the Moabite"—keeping the outsider's identity before us even now, at the moment redemption is dawning, so that the grace of her inclusion never loses its wonder. Ruth adds a further detail of Boaz's kindness that she had not yet reported: he invited her to "keep close" to his workers "until they have finished all my harvest." This was an extraordinary provision. It meant that Ruth's gleaning was not to be a single day's mercy but a season-long security—she could glean safely in Boaz's fields through the entire barley and wheat harvests, several weeks of guaranteed provision. The Hebrew text actually has Boaz saying "keep close to my young men," which Naomi will gently amend in the next verse for Ruth's protection. But the point Ruth grasps is the duration and reliability of Boaz's care. This is not a one-time handout but an ongoing covenant of provision. Carson notes how the cumulative weight of Boaz's kindnesses—protection, water, a meal, extra grain, and now season-long welcome—builds an overwhelming portrait of generosity that goes far beyond duty. Ruth, in her innocent reporting, does not fully understand the redemptive significance of all this; she simply rejoices in the practical security it brings. But Naomi, hearing it, sees the larger pattern. The redeemer is not merely generous for a day; he means to sustain them through the whole harvest. And in that sustained provision, the seed of a far greater redemption is quietly germinating.

verseByVerse.quote: And Naomi said to Ruth, her daughter-in-law, "It is good, my daughter, that you go out with his young women, lest in another field you be assaulted." So she kept close to the young women of Boaz, gleaning until the end of the barley and wheat harvests. And she lived with her mother-in-law. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Naomi, now alert and engaged where before she had been passive in grief, gives wise and protective counsel. She gently corrects Boaz's words: rather than keeping close to the young men, Ruth should stay with "his young women"—for a vulnerable foreign widow, the company of the women was safer, "lest in another field you be assaulted." Naomi's renewed concern for Ruth's safety shows how fully her heart has reengaged with life and hope; the woman who once urged Ruth away now plans carefully for her good. The chapter then closes with a summary that spans weeks: Ruth "kept close to the young women of Boaz, gleaning until the end of the barley and wheat harvests." The barley harvest began in spring and the wheat harvest followed, so this covers roughly two months of faithful, daily labor and of Boaz's faithful, daily provision. And the final clause is quietly significant: "And she lived with her mother-in-law." Ruth did not drift away once provision was secured; she remained faithful to her vow, dwelling with Naomi, serving her still. Wenham notes that this closing line of stability and continued loyalty sets the stage perfectly for chapter 3, where the question will shift from daily bread to permanent rest—from gleaning to redemption, from survival to a home. The harvest is gathered; the redeemer is identified; the two faithful women dwell together in hope. The narrator has filled the empty barns and the empty hearts. Now he will move to fill the empty future.

2.theology:
The Hidden Providence of God. Chapter 2 unveils how God's sovereignty ordinarily operates—not chiefly through spectacular miracle but through 'coincidence' and the faithful obedience of ordinary people. The narrator's deliberately ironic phrase, 'she happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz' (v. 3), teaches that in God's universe there is no such thing as luck. What Ruth experiences as chance is the orchestration of a sovereign Lord who has already positioned her redeemer (v. 1). Behind every 'coincidence' that shapes our lives stands the unobserved hand of God, weaving redemption.

Grace Beyond Law. Boaz embodies a generosity that vastly exceeds legal requirement. The gleaning laws (Lev 19:9–10; Deut 24:19–22) set a minimum floor of provision for the poor; Boaz commands his workers to leave 'handfuls on purpose' (v. 16), lavishing on Ruth far more than the law demanded. This is the gospel pattern: the law establishes a floor, but grace knows no ceiling. God does not deal with his people according to strict legal measure but pours out abundance we could never earn.

The Refuge of God's Wings. Boaz's blessing in v. 12—'under whose wings (kanaf) you have come to take refuge'—presents one of Scripture's tenderest images of God as a sheltering mother bird. This is the picture of saving faith: fleeing to God for refuge. The image culminates on the lips of Jesus, who longed to gather Jerusalem 'as a hen gathers her brood under her wings' (Matt 23:37). Astonishingly, Boaz will himself become the answer to his prayer when Ruth asks him to spread his 'wings' over her (3:9).
2.examples:
Then: Gleaning was Israel's social safety net for the poor, the widow, the orphan, and the foreigner—a divinely mandated provision that required landowners to leave the edges and droppings of their fields for the destitute. It was honest but humbling labor, and dangerous for a vulnerable foreign woman alone in the fields. Boaz's protection of Ruth from harassment, his provision of water and food, and his command to leave extra grain all went far beyond what the law required, modeling the heart of God toward the marginalized.

Now: Boaz challenges us to let faith saturate the ordinary spheres of work and business. His first words to his laborers are a blessing; his treatment of a powerless outsider overflows with dignity and generosity. He shows us that godliness is most credible precisely where it is hardest—in the marketplace, in our treatment of those who can do nothing for us. The hidden providence of God so often reaches the vulnerable through the open hands of his obedient people. We are called to be the 'handfuls on purpose' that God leaves in the fields of a hurting world—and to remember, with Ruth's wonder, 'Why have I found favor in your eyes?' before the grace that found us when we had no claim.

3.title: The Bold Request
3.text: <sup>9</sup>He said, "Who are you?" And she answered, "I am Ruth, your servant. Spread your wings over your servant, for you are a redeemer." (ESV)
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is the daring heart of the book, a scene charged with tension, tenderness, and theological weight. The barley and wheat harvests are over; the season of gleaning has ended, and with it the temporary provision that sustained Ruth and Naomi. Now Naomi—fully revived from her bitterness and thinking once more like a mother—conceives a bold and risky plan to secure not merely bread for Ruth but "rest," a home, a permanent future (3:1). She sends Ruth to the threshing floor by night, to the place where Boaz will be sleeping after the winnowing, to make an audacious request.

The scene at the threshing floor is fraught with cultural and moral delicacy. A woman approaching a man at night, uncovering his feet, lying down beside him—the situation is loaded with potential for scandal. Yet the narrator is careful to present both Ruth and Boaz as people of sterling integrity. Ruth's request, when it comes, is not seduction but a marriage proposal couched in the language of covenant and redemption: "Spread your wings over your servant, for you are a redeemer" (3:9). This is the most theologically loaded request in the entire book. The word for "wings" (kanaf) is the very word Boaz had used in 2:12 when he prayed that Ruth would be rewarded by the God under whose "wings" she had taken refuge. Now Ruth, with stunning boldness, asks Boaz to become the human answer to his own prayer—to spread his wing of protection, his covering, over her in marriage and redemption.

Boaz's response is one of the most beautiful in Scripture. There is no offense, no exploitation, no hesitation born of self-interest. Instead he blesses her: "May you be blessed by the LORD, my daughter. You have made this last kindness greater than the first" (3:10). He honors her, calls her a "worthy woman" (3:11)—the female counterpart to his own description as a "worthy man" in 2:1—and commits himself to act as her redeemer. But there is a complication: a nearer kinsman exists who has the prior right of redemption (3:12). Boaz, scrupulously just, will not act outside the proper order. He sends Ruth home before dawn with a generous gift of grain and a promise: he will settle the matter that very day.

As Keller and Ferguson both observe, this chapter dramatizes the gospel posture of the soul. Ruth comes to her redeemer not in pride but in lowliness, not claiming her worth but appealing to his role: "you are a redeemer." She rests her whole future on his willingness to cover her. And Boaz, the worthy redeemer, receives her appeal with delight and pledges himself to her cause. So the believing soul comes to Christ—not with merit, but with the bold confidence that he is the Redeemer, casting itself entirely upon his grace and his covering wings.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With the harvest ended, Naomi—now thinking of Ruth's permanent security—devises a plan. She instructs Ruth to wash, anoint herself, dress well, and go secretly to the threshing floor at night, to lie at Boaz's feet and let him direct what follows. Ruth agrees to do all that Naomi says.
verseByVerse.theology: Naomi seeks 'rest' (menuhah) for Ruth—a settled home, security, a future. This is the same 'rest' she had prayed for in 1:9. The plan, though culturally bold and morally precarious, is aimed at invoking the law of the kinsman-redeemer and levirate marriage to secure both Ruth's future and the preservation of Elimelech's line. Naomi's transformation from despairing widow to active matchmaker shows faith reengaging with hope and taking responsible action under God's providence.
verseByVerse.examples: Naomi seeks not merely Ruth's survival but her flourishing—not just bread but a home. Genuine love for others looks beyond immediate needs to lasting good. Yet the plan also carries real risk and ambiguity, reminding us that faithful people act within imperfect circumstances, trusting God to govern the outcome. Wisdom and faith work together; Naomi plans shrewdly while the result rests in God's hands.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Naomi her mother-in-law said to her, "My daughter, should I not seek rest for you, that it may be well with you?" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter opens with Naomi taking the initiative—a striking contrast to the passive, grief-stricken woman of chapter 1. "Should I not seek rest for you, that it may be well with you?" The word "rest" (manoah) is rich; it means a settled home, security, a permanent place of belonging and provision. It is the very thing Naomi had prayed for back in 1:9, when she asked the LORD to grant her daughters-in-law "rest, each of you in the house of her husband." Now Naomi sets out to become the instrument of that prayer's fulfillment. Her motive is selfless love: she seeks Ruth's good, that it may be "well" with her. Begg observes that this is the mark of redeemed love—not seeking merely the temporary relief of gleaning but the lasting security of a home and a future. Naomi has come a long way from "call me Mara." The woman who felt the Almighty had emptied her now busies herself filling the future of the daughter who would not leave her. There is also a deeper theology stirring here. The "rest" Naomi seeks for Ruth is a foreshadowing of the rest the gospel offers—the settled, secure belonging that comes through redemption. As Augustine famously prayed, our hearts are restless until they find their rest in God. Naomi, perhaps without fully knowing it, is reaching toward the great theme of redemptive rest that the whole story is moving to provide.

verseByVerse.quote: "Is not Boaz our relative, with whose young women you were? See, he is winnowing barley tonight at the threshing floor. Wash therefore and anoint yourself, and put on your cloak and go down to the threshing floor, but do not make yourself known to the man until he has finished eating and drinking. But when he lies down, observe the place where he lies. Then go and uncover his feet and lie down, and he will tell you what to do." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Naomi's plan is detailed, bold, and culturally loaded. She reminds Ruth that Boaz is "our relative"—a go'el, with the right and duty of redemption—and notes that he will be at the threshing floor that night, winnowing barley. The threshing floor was where grain was separated from chaff by tossing it into the evening breeze; landowners often slept there at harvest time to guard the precious heaps. Naomi instructs Ruth to prepare herself—"wash... anoint yourself, and put on your cloak"—the language suggests a woman preparing for a significant encounter, perhaps even removing the garments of mourning to present herself as a bride-to-be. She is to wait until Boaz has eaten and lain down, then quietly "uncover his feet and lie down." The scene is undeniably charged with potential for scandal—a woman approaching a sleeping man at night. Yet Wenham and other careful commentators stress that the action, understood within its cultural framework, is not seductive but a recognized, if daring, appeal for marriage and redemption. The uncovering of the feet and lying down was a symbolic gesture inviting Boaz to extend his protection. "He will tell you what to do"—Naomi trusts Boaz's integrity to direct the encounter rightly. The plan walks a knife's edge of risk and propriety, and its success depends entirely on the character of both Ruth and Boaz. Naomi is gambling everything on the godliness of a worthy man—and on the providence of God.

verseByVerse.quote: And she replied, "All that you say I will do." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Ruth's answer is the answer of complete trust and submission: "All that you say I will do."
