There is no hesitation, no objection, no calculation of the risk to her reputation or her safety. The same loyal love (hesed) that bound her to Naomi at the crossroads in chapter 1 now governs her obedience to Naomi's bold plan. Ruth has cast her lot entirely with Naomi and Naomi's God, and she trusts her mother-in-law's wisdom even when the path is fraught with danger and uncertainty. This is a remarkable display of the trust that exists between these two women, forged in shared suffering and sealed by covenant loyalty. Ferguson notes that Ruth's willingness to do "all" that Naomi says reflects the obedience of faith—a willingness to step into a risky and unclear situation, trusting the guidance she has been given and the God who governs the outcome. There is also a quiet courage here that should not be missed. Ruth, a foreign widow with everything to lose and only her reputation to protect, agrees to a plan that could be catastrophically misunderstood. She does so because she trusts both Naomi and the God under whose wings she has taken refuge. The Septuagint and several Hebrew manuscripts add "to me" — "all that you say to me I will do" — underscoring the personal, covenantal nature of her submission. The destitute Moabite is about to walk by faith into the dark, trusting that the God of Israel will not let her fall.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ruth goes to the threshing floor and waits until Boaz lies down. At midnight he wakes, startled to find a woman at his feet. Ruth identifies herself and makes her bold request: 'Spread your wings over your servant, for you are a redeemer.' Boaz responds with blessing and honor, pledging to redeem her—but reveals that a nearer kinsman has the prior right.
verseByVerse.theology: The theological center of the book occurs here. Ruth's request—'spread your wings (kanaf) over your servant, for you are a redeemer (go'el)'—uses the exact word Boaz had used in 2:12 of God's protective wings. Ruth is asking Boaz to become the human means by which God's protective covering is extended to her. Boaz's response models the willing redeemer: he does not exploit, does not hesitate from self-interest, but blesses her and commits to act—while honoring the prior claim of the nearer kinsman, showing that redemption proceeds in righteousness.
verseByVerse.examples: Ruth comes to her redeemer not claiming worth but appealing to his role: 'you are a redeemer.' This is the posture of saving faith—casting oneself wholly upon the redeemer's willingness and grace. Boaz, for his part, models the integrity of one who could exploit a vulnerable woman in the dark but instead protects her honor and acts justly. True redemption is never coerced or compromised; it is freely given and righteously accomplished.

verseByVerse.quote: So she went down to the threshing floor and did just as her mother-in-law had commanded her. And when Boaz had eaten and drunk, and his heart was merry, he went to lie down at the end of the heap of grain. Then she came softly and uncovered his feet and lay down. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Ruth carries out the plan with quiet courage—"she did just as her mother-in-law had commanded her." The scene is set with vivid, almost cinematic detail. Boaz, after the labor of winnowing, eats and drinks, and "his heart was merry"—a phrase that simply means he was content and satisfied, not drunk (the narrator is careful to preserve Boaz's dignity and sobriety, lest we suspect any impropriety). He lies down to sleep "at the end of the heap of grain," guarding the precious harvest through the night. Then comes the tense moment: "she came softly"—stealthily, silently, so as not to wake him or attract notice—"and uncovered his feet and lay down." Every word here is charged with risk. A single misstep, a single misunderstanding, could ruin Ruth's reputation and Naomi's hopes forever. The darkness of the threshing floor, the sleeping man, the woman at his feet—the narrator deliberately holds us in suspense. Wenham notes the masterful tension: we know Ruth's intentions are honorable and Naomi's plan aims at marriage, but the situation is undeniably precarious and could be read in the worst light. Yet the narrator has carefully established the integrity of both characters, so that we trust this will resolve in righteousness. Ruth has done the bold thing faith required; now she lies in the dark and waits, her whole future hanging on what the worthy man will do when he wakes. The stage is set for the most important conversation in the book.

verseByVerse.quote: At midnight the man was startled and turned over, and behold, a woman lay at his feet! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The narrator builds the suspense with a single dramatic verse. "At midnight"—the deepest dark, the most vulnerable hour—"the man was startled." The Hebrew suggests a sudden shudder, a trembling; perhaps the night had grown cold, or some movement disturbed him. He "turned over, and behold, a woman lay at his feet!" The narrator's "behold" places us inside Boaz's startled awareness: he wakes to discover, to his complete astonishment, that a woman is lying at his feet in the dark. The moment is electric with possibility and danger. Boaz does not know who she is or why she is there; the situation could be interpreted in any number of ways, most of them scandalous. This is the hinge on which the entire chapter—and arguably the whole book—turns. How will this worthy man respond to finding a woman at his feet at midnight, when no one is watching, when he could do anything? The narrator has deliberately constructed a scene of maximum moral peril precisely to display the integrity that follows. Carson notes that the storyteller's art here is consummate: he holds us in breathless uncertainty before resolving everything into honor and blessing. The darkness of the threshing floor will become the stage on which Ruth's faith and Boaz's righteousness shine all the brighter. And the question "Who are you?" which Boaz is about to ask, will open the door to the most theologically rich exchange in the book.

verseByVerse.quote: He said, "Who are you?" And she answered, "I am Ruth, your servant. Spread your wings over your servant, for you are a redeemer." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Here is the theological summit of the entire book, and it deserves to be lingered over with wonder. Boaz asks, "Who are you?" and Ruth's answer is a masterpiece of humble boldness: "I am Ruth, your servant. Spread your wings over your servant, for you are a redeemer." Every phrase is freighted with meaning. First, she names herself "your servant"—not presuming on any status, casting herself in lowliness before him. Then comes the breathtaking request: "Spread your wings over your servant." The word for "wings" is kanaf—and it is the very same word Boaz had used in 2:12, when he prayed that the LORD, "under whose wings you have come to take refuge," would reward her. Now Ruth, with stunning theological insight and courage, takes Boaz's own prayer and turns it back upon him: you prayed that I would find refuge under God's wings—now you spread your wing of covering over me. She asks him to become the human means by which God answers his own prayer. To "spread one's wing" (or skirt, the corner of one's garment) over a woman was an idiom for marriage and protection (cf. Ezek 16:8). And she grounds her appeal not in her worthiness but in his role: "for you are a redeemer"—a go'el. Keller's exposition is unforgettable here: Ruth does not come pleading her merits; she comes claiming his identity. "You are a redeemer"—therefore redeem me. This is precisely how the soul comes to Christ: not 'I am worthy,' but 'You are the Redeemer; spread your wings over me.'

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "May you be blessed by the LORD, my daughter. You have made this last kindness greater than the first in that you have not gone after young men, whether poor or rich." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Boaz's response melts away all the tension of the scene and reveals the heart of a truly noble man. There is no offense, no exploitation, no suspicion—only blessing. "May you be blessed by the LORD, my daughter." He addresses her tenderly, as he did in chapter 2, and his first instinct is to invoke God's blessing upon her. Then he honors her astonishing loyalty: "You have made this last kindness greater than the first." The word is again hesed—loyal, covenant love. The "first" kindness was Ruth's faithfulness to Naomi, leaving her homeland to care for her widowed mother-in-law; the "last" and even greater kindness is this—that Ruth, a young woman, has sought to marry an older kinsman in order to preserve the family line of her dead husband and provide for Naomi, rather than pursuing romance with "young men, whether poor or rich." Boaz recognizes that Ruth could easily have sought a husband among the young men of Bethlehem; instead, she has subordinated her own desires to the cause of family loyalty and redemption. Ferguson notes the beauty of Boaz's character: a lesser man might have been flattered or might have taken advantage; Boaz is humbled and grateful, and his thought is entirely for Ruth's honor and welfare. He sees her request not as forward but as the crowning act of her self-giving hesed. In a single verse, Boaz transforms a potentially scandalous midnight encounter into a covenant of honor and blessing. The worthy man has met the worthy woman, and grace abounds.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, my daughter, do not fear. I will do for you all that you ask, for all my fellow townsmen know that you are a worthy woman. And now it is true that I am a redeemer. Yet there is a redeemer nearer than I. Remain tonight, and in the morning, if he will redeem you, good; let him do it. But if he is not willing to redeem you, then, as the LORD lives, I will redeem you. Lie down until the morning." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Boaz's words are a model of pastoral tenderness, integrity, and resolve. "Do not fear"—he calms her anxiety. "I will do for you all that you ask"—he commits himself to her cause. And he honors her publicly in his heart: "all my fellow townsmen know that you are a worthy woman." The phrase "worthy woman" (eshet hayil) is the precise female counterpart to the "worthy man" (gibbor hayil) that described Boaz himself in 2:1—and it is the same phrase that crowns the virtuous woman of Proverbs 31:10. The narrator is signaling a perfect match: the worthy man and the worthy woman belong together. But then Boaz reveals a complication that displays his scrupulous justice: "there is a redeemer nearer than I." There exists a kinsman with a prior legal claim, and Boaz, righteous man that he is, will not seize the role of redeemer by bypassing the proper order. He will give the nearer kinsman his rightful first opportunity. Yet his commitment to Ruth is unconditional and sealed with an oath: "as the LORD lives, I will redeem you" if the other will not. Keller draws out the gospel foreshadowing: there is a nearer redeemer who has the right but, as chapter 4 will show, lacks the willingness. The law itself is like that nearer kinsman—it has a prior claim on us, but it cannot ultimately redeem; only the willing Redeemer can. Boaz sends Ruth to "lie down until the morning"—safe, honored, and now bound to him by promise.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ruth lies at Boaz's feet until before dawn, then rises to avoid scandal. Boaz sends her home with six measures of barley—a generous pledge of his intentions and a gift for Naomi. Naomi, hearing all, assures Ruth that Boaz will not rest until the matter is settled that very day.
verseByVerse.theology: Boaz's gift of six measures of barley is a token of his commitment—a pledge that he will provide and will not send Ruth back to Naomi empty. It echoes and answers Naomi's complaint in 1:21 that the LORD brought her back 'empty'; now grain after grain fills her house. Naomi's closing words, 'the man will not rest until he has settled the matter today,' reveal her confidence in Boaz's character and her trust that redemption is now in motion. The chapter ends in expectant rest, awaiting the redeemer's decisive action.
verseByVerse.examples: Boaz's integrity in sending Ruth away before dawn—protecting her reputation and his own—models the care that genuine love takes for the honor of the beloved. And his gift of grain shows that true commitment expresses itself in tangible provision, not mere words. Naomi's counsel to 'wait' teaches the patience of faith: having done all, we rest in the faithfulness of the redeemer to complete what he has promised.

verseByVerse.quote: So she lay at his feet until the morning, but arose before one could recognize another. And he said, "Let it not be known that the woman came to the threshing floor." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Ruth lies at Boaz's feet through the remainder of the night—in complete propriety, the narrator is careful to make clear—and "arose before one could recognize another," rising in the gray dawn before there was enough light for anyone to identify her. Boaz's words reveal his careful concern for both Ruth's reputation and the integrity of the redemption process: "Let it not be known that the woman came to the threshing floor." This is not the secrecy of guilt but the wisdom of honor. Boaz knows how easily this innocent encounter could be misinterpreted by gossiping tongues, and he guards Ruth's name as zealously as his own. There is a deep tenderness and protectiveness in this; the worthy man shields the worthy woman from any breath of scandal. Wenham notes that throughout this chapter the narrator takes pains to establish the spotless character of both parties—nothing improper has occurred, and Boaz's first concern upon waking and upon parting is for Ruth's honor. This care for reputation also serves the larger redemptive purpose: if word spread of a midnight tryst, it could jeopardize the lawful, public redemption that Boaz intends to pursue at the city gate. So Boaz protects not only Ruth's name but the very possibility of her redemption. There is a quiet beauty in a love that thinks first of the beloved's honor, that guards what is precious, that will not let even the appearance of evil cloud the path to a righteous union.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Bring the garment you are wearing and hold it out." So she held it, and he measured out six measures of barley and put it on her. Then she went into the city. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Before sending Ruth home, Boaz gives her a substantial gift: "six measures of barley," poured into the garment she held out. The exact quantity is uncertain, but it was a generous load—heavy enough that he had to lift it onto her. This gift is far more than a kindness; it is a pledge, a token of Boaz's serious intent and a sign that he will follow through on his promise. Crucially, it ensures that Ruth will not return to Naomi empty-handed. The narrator surely intends us to hear the echo of Naomi's bitter complaint in 1:21: "I went away full, and the LORD has brought me back empty." The woman who declared herself empty is now receiving, measure after measure, the filling of grace. Boaz will not send Ruth—or Naomi—back empty. Begg observes the symbolic weight: the redeemer's gift is both provision and promise, a down payment on the full redemption to come. There may also be intentional symbolism in the number six, perhaps pointing toward completion to follow, or simply a generous measure that Ruth could carry. Whatever the precise meaning, the gesture speaks of a redeemer who gives lavishly and binds himself to his word with tangible pledges. "Then she went into the city"—carrying not only barley but hope, returning to Naomi with evidence in her arms that the redeemer means to act. The empty house is being filled, grain by grain, with the firstfruits of redemption.

verseByVerse.quote: And when she came to her mother-in-law, she said, "How did you fare, my daughter?" Then she told her all that the man had done for her, saying, "These six measures of barley he gave to me, for he said to me, 'You must not go back empty-handed to your mother-in-law.'" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Ruth returns to Naomi, who greets her with an eager question—literally in the Hebrew, "Who are you, my daughter?"—perhaps asking in the dim light, or more likely asking in effect, "How did it go? What is your status now—are you betrothed?" Ruth recounts "all that the man had done for her" and presents the six measures of barley with Boaz's own words attached: "You must not go back empty-handed to your mother-in-law." This is a precious detail, for it shows that Boaz's generosity was directed not only toward Ruth but toward Naomi as well. The redeemer's care reaches the whole family. And those words—"not... empty-handed"—land with theological force. Naomi had returned from Moab declaring herself empty (1:21); now the redeemer explicitly refuses to let her remain so. The very emptiness she lamented is being reversed by the kindness of Boaz, who functions as the agent of God's filling grace. Carson notes how the narrator weaves the language of fullness and emptiness throughout the book, and here the redeemer's stated intention—that Naomi not go back empty—signals that the great reversal is well underway. The God who emptied is now, through his chosen redeemer, filling. Ruth's report is not merely a recounting of events but a proclamation of hope: the man has acted, the man has given, the man has pledged that emptiness will not have the last word. Naomi, who once tasted only bitterness, now hears from the redeemer himself the promise of fullness.

verseByVerse.quote: She replied, "Wait, my daughter, until you learn how the matter turns out, for the man will not rest until he has settled the matter today." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Naomi's closing counsel is the perfect note on which to end the chapter: "Wait... until you learn how the matter turns out." Having done all that faith and shrewdness required, there is now nothing left for Ruth to do but rest in the redeemer's faithfulness. This is the patience of faith—the quiet confidence that, the matter being now in the hands of a worthy redeemer, the outcome is secure. And Naomi's reason for this confidence is a magnificent testimony to Boaz's character: "the man will not rest until he has settled the matter today." Naomi knows Boaz; she knows his integrity, his resolve, his commitment. He is not the kind of man who delays or wavers or forgets; having pledged himself, he will pursue the redemption to its completion that very day. Ferguson draws the gospel parallel beautifully: the believer's rest is grounded not in his own efforts but in the unwavering commitment of the Redeemer to finish what he has begun. "He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion" (Phil 1:6). Just as Boaz will not rest until Ruth is redeemed, so Christ will not rest until his people are fully and finally his. There is a holy restlessness in the heart of every true redeemer—a refusal to leave the work half-done. So the chapter of the bold request ends not in anxiety but in restful expectation: the redeemer is at work, and he will not stop until the matter is settled. The bride waits in peace, for everything now depends on the faithfulness of the one who has pledged to redeem her.

3.theology:
The Willing Redeemer. At the threshing floor, Ruth appeals to Boaz not on the basis of her worth but on the basis of his identity: 'you are a redeemer' (v. 9). Boaz responds not with reluctance or exploitation but with blessing, honor, and an unconditional pledge sealed by oath (vv. 10–13). This willingness is the very heart of the book's Christology. A redeemer must have the right, the resources, and—crucially—the willingness to redeem. Boaz did not have to redeem Ruth; he chose to, out of love and honor. So Christ, the eternal Son with every right and infinite resources, was supremely willing: 'I delight to do your will, O my God' (Ps 40:8).

Spread Your Wings: The Prayer Answered Through the Pray-er. Ruth's request that Boaz 'spread your wings (kanaf) over your servant' (v. 9) deliberately echoes Boaz's own prayer in 2:12 that the LORD, 'under whose wings you have come to take refuge,' would reward her. Ruth asks Boaz to become the human means by which God answers his own prayer. This is a profound picture of how God works: he often answers our prayers for others by making us the instrument of the very blessing we requested. The wings of divine refuge are spread through the obedient covering of God's people—and supremely through Christ, who gathers his own under his wings (Matt 23:37).

The Posture of Saving Faith. Ruth comes to her redeemer in lowliness ('your servant'), in boldness ('spread your wings over me'), and in confident appeal to his role ('you are a redeemer'). This is precisely the posture of the soul coming to Christ: not pleading merit but claiming his identity as Savior, casting itself wholly upon his willingness and grace. We do not say to Christ, 'I am worthy'; we say, 'You are the Redeemer—cover me.'
3.examples:
Then: The threshing floor at harvest was a place where landowners slept to guard their grain, and the cultural conventions surrounding the kinsman-redeemer and levirate marriage (Lev 25:25; Deut 25:5–10) framed Ruth's bold approach. Her request that Boaz spread his garment over her was a recognized idiom for marriage and protection. The scene, fraught with potential for scandal, was navigated by both parties with scrupulous integrity—Ruth in her honorable intent, Boaz in his protection of her reputation and his refusal to bypass the nearer kinsman's lawful claim.

Now: Ruth teaches us how to come to our Redeemer—not with pride in our achievements but with the bold humility that says, 'You are the Redeemer; spread your wings over me.' We approach Christ empty-handed, appealing not to our worth but to his role and his willingness. Boaz, meanwhile, models a love that guards the honor of the beloved, that acts in righteousness rather than seizing advantage, and that gives tangible pledges of commitment. And Naomi's counsel to 'wait' until the redeemer settles the matter teaches the restful patience of faith: having done all, we trust the One who 'will not rest until he has settled the matter,' confident that he who began a good work will complete it.

4.title: The Redeemer Steps Forward
4.text: <sup>13</sup>So Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife. And he went in to her, and the LORD gave her conception, and she bore a son... <sup>17</sup>...They named him Obed. He was the father of Jesse, the father of David. (ESV)
4.overview:
Chapter 4 brings the story to its glorious resolution at the gate of Bethlehem—the place of legal transaction and public witness in an Israelite town. Boaz, true to Naomi's confidence that he would not rest until the matter was settled, goes up to the gate and convenes the necessary legal proceedings before the elders and the people. The chapter is structured as a courtroom drama, and at its center stands a striking contrast between two redeemers: the nearer kinsman who has the prior right but ultimately lacks the willingness, and Boaz, who steps forward with wholehearted resolve.

The nearer redeemer is willing enough to redeem the land—until he learns that redeeming the land means also marrying Ruth and raising up an heir who would carry the name of the dead and inherit the very property he sought to acquire. "I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I impair my own inheritance" (4:6). His calculation is self-protective; the cost to himself is too great. And so, in one of the most theologically resonant moments in the book, the nearer redeemer steps back, and Boaz steps forward. As Keller and Sproul both observe, this nameless kinsman represents the law itself: the law has a prior and legitimate claim upon us—we are lawbreakers—but the law cannot redeem us, for to do so would 'impair its own inheritance,' compromising its righteous demands. Only a redeemer willing to bear the cost himself can save. Boaz is that redeemer: "I will redeem her."

The sandal ceremony seals the transaction, the elders pronounce their blessing, and Boaz takes Ruth as his wife. Then comes the climactic verse: "the LORD gave her conception, and she bore a son" (4:13). After ten years of barrenness in Moab, after the deaths and the emptiness, God opens Ruth's womb—and the narrator is careful to attribute the conception directly to the LORD. The God who seemed hidden, who emptied Naomi and brought her back bitter, is revealed as the God who fills, who redeems, who gives life where there was death. The women of Bethlehem proclaim that this child is a 'restorer of life' to Naomi, and they place him in the lap of the woman who once cried 'call me Mara.' The empty arms are full at last.

And then the genealogy—which transforms this intimate village story into a hinge of redemptive history. The child is Obed, who fathered Jesse, who fathered David. The little story of a Moabite widow and a worthy redeemer turns out to be a vital link in the chain that leads to Israel's greatest king—and, as Matthew 1:5 will reveal, to David's greater Son, the Lord Jesus Christ. Ruth the Moabite, the outsider drawn under the wings of grace, stands in the genealogy of the Messiah. The barley field outside Bethlehem has led us, by hidden providence, all the way to the manger of Bethlehem. The gospel in miniature is complete.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Boaz goes to the city gate and summons the nearer kinsman before ten elders. He presents the matter of redeeming Naomi's land. The nearer kinsman agrees—until he learns that redemption includes marrying Ruth to raise up an heir for the dead, which would impair his own inheritance. He declines and yields the right of redemption to Boaz.
verseByVerse.theology: The nearer kinsman represents the principle that redemption requires not only right and resources but willingness. He has the legal right (he is the nearer go'el) and presumably the resources, but when the full cost is revealed, he will not pay it. Many commentators see in him a picture of the law: it has a prior, legitimate claim on us as lawbreakers, but it cannot redeem—to do so would 'impair its own inheritance,' compromising its righteous demands. Only a redeemer willing to bear the cost can save.
verseByVerse.examples: The nearer kinsman is the prudent man, the calculating man, who weighs the cost of redemption against his own interest and finds it too high. He is not wicked; he is simply unwilling to be diminished for another's sake. He stands in contrast to every true redeemer who counts the beloved worth the cost. His self-protective 'I cannot... lest I impair my own inheritance' is the antithesis of the gospel's self-giving love.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Boaz had gone up to the gate and sat down there. And behold, the redeemer, of whom Boaz had spoken, came by. So Boaz said, "Turn aside, friend; sit down here." And he turned aside and sat down. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: True to Naomi's word that he would not rest, Boaz "had gone up to the gate"—the public square just inside the city walls where legal business, commerce, and judicial matters were conducted in an Israelite town. This was the appropriate, lawful venue for the redemption transaction; Boaz does everything openly, in proper order, before legitimate witnesses. And again the narrator's "behold" signals providence at work: "the redeemer, of whom Boaz had spoken, came by" at precisely the right moment. As with Ruth's arrival in Boaz's field (2:3) and Boaz's arrival from Bethlehem (2:4), the timing is no accident; the sovereign God who orchestrated every step of this story now brings the nearer kinsman across Boaz's path at the exact hour needed. Boaz calls to him, "Turn aside, friend; sit down here." Interestingly, the Hebrew here for "friend" is a curious idiom (peloni almoni), something like "so-and-so" or "such a one"—a deliberate way of leaving the man unnamed. Wenham and others note the narrator's pointed choice: the man who would not redeem, who would not bear the cost to preserve the name of the dead, is himself left nameless in the record, while Boaz and Ruth are honored forever. There is a quiet justice in this anonymity. The one who refused to perpetuate another's name forfeits his own. The redeemer who steps forward will be remembered; the one who steps back is forgotten.

verseByVerse.quote: And he took ten men of the elders of the city and said, "Sit down here." So they sat down. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Boaz convenes a formal legal assembly: "he took ten men of the elders of the city." In Israelite practice, the elders served as witnesses and judges for important legal transactions, and the number ten appears to have constituted a recognized quorum for such public business (a tradition that continued into later Jewish practice as the minyan). Boaz is meticulous in following proper procedure. He does not act rashly or in secret; he assembles legitimate witnesses so that whatever is decided will be binding, public, and beyond dispute. This careful legality reflects Boaz's character throughout the book—a man of integrity who does things rightly, in the open, according to the law. It also serves the redemptive purpose: Ruth's redemption must be unimpeachable, secured by proper witnesses so that the marriage and the child to come will be fully legitimate in the eyes of the community. Begg notes that Boaz's scrupulous attention to legal form is itself a kind of love—he is ensuring that Ruth's status, and the status of any child born to them, will be entirely secure and honorable. There is no shortcut here, no cutting of corners. The redeemer wants the redemption to be perfect, complete, legally airtight. The elders sit; the court is convened; the stage is set for the decisive transaction. And we sense the narrator's deliberate building of solemnity—this is no mere village negotiation but a moment that will echo down the generations, witnessed by the elders of Bethlehem and, unbeknownst to them, by all of redemptive history.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to the redeemer, "Naomi, who has come back from the country of Moab, is selling the parcel of land that belonged to our relative Elimelech. So I thought I would tell you of it and say, 'Buy it in the presence of those sitting here and in the presence of the elders of my people.' If you will redeem it, redeem it. But if you will not, tell me, that I may know, for there is no one besides you to redeem it, and I come after you." And he said, "I will redeem it." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Boaz opens the proceedings strategically. He begins not with Ruth but with the matter of land: Naomi is selling (or offering for redemption) a parcel that belonged to Elimelech. Under the law of redemption (Lev 25:25), the nearest kinsman had the right and duty to buy back family land to keep it within the clan. Boaz lays the matter plainly before the nearer redeemer, scrupulously honoring his prior claim: "If you will redeem it, redeem it." He acknowledges the proper order: "there is no one besides you to redeem it, and I come after you." Boaz could have schemed to bypass the nearer kinsman, but his integrity will not permit it; he gives the man the first and rightful opportunity. The kinsman, hearing only of the land—a profitable acquisition that would enlarge his holdings—readily agrees: "I will redeem it." At this point the redemption looks like a straightforward gain for him: he acquires good land at the cost of the redemption price. There is no hint yet of the complication to come. Wenham notes the narrator's dramatic skill in withholding the crucial condition; the kinsman commits himself to redeem before he learns the full cost. This is how Boaz has arranged it—first establishing the man's willingness regarding the land, then revealing the burden that comes attached. The trap of self-interest is being gently sprung. The man who will redeem for gain is about to discover that true redemption costs more than he is willing to pay.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Boaz said, "The day you buy the field from the hand of Naomi, you also acquire Ruth the Moabite, the widow of the dead, in order to perpetuate the name of the dead in his inheritance." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Now Boaz reveals the full cost, and everything changes. To redeem the land is not merely to acquire property; it is also to "acquire Ruth the Moabite, the widow of the dead, in order to perpetuate the name of the dead in his inheritance." Here the law of land redemption (Lev 25) intersects with the principle of levirate marriage (Deut 25:5–10): the redeemer must marry Ruth and raise up a son who would carry the name and inherit the property of the dead—Mahlon, Ruth's first husband, and ultimately Elimelech's line. This transforms the transaction utterly. The land would not become a permanent addition to the redeemer's estate; rather, the firstborn son of his union with Ruth would inherit it as the heir of the dead. The redeemer would bear the cost of the redemption price, the cost of supporting Ruth and the child, and yet the land would pass to that child's line, not enrich his own. And once more the narrator pointedly calls her "Ruth the Moabite"—the outsider label persisting to the very end, making her ultimate inclusion in the line of David all the more a wonder of grace. Sproul observes the brilliant theological pattern emerging: redemption that costs nothing is no redemption at all. The nearer kinsman was glad to redeem when it meant gain; he will recoil when it means genuine, self-diminishing sacrifice. The true price of redemption is about to expose the difference between a redeemer who calculates and a redeemer who loves.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the redeemer said, "I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I impair my own inheritance. Take my right of redemption yourself, for I cannot redeem it." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: And there it is—the great refusal, the moment the nearer redeemer steps back. "I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I impair my own inheritance." His reasoning is entirely self-protective: to redeem Ruth and raise up an heir for the dead would diminish his own estate and complicate his own family's inheritance. The cost is too high. He is not portrayed as wicked—merely prudent, calculating, unwilling to be diminished for another's sake. "Take my right of redemption yourself, for I cannot redeem it." He surrenders his claim, and in doing so he steps out of the story forever, nameless. This is one of the most theologically luminous moments in all of Scripture, and the great commentators seize upon it. Keller's exposition is unforgettable: this nameless kinsman represents the law. The law has a prior and legitimate claim upon us—we are lawbreakers, and the law's demand is just. But the law cannot redeem us, for to do so would 'impair its own inheritance'—it would have to compromise its righteous requirements, and this it cannot do. The law can condemn; it cannot save. And so, when the law steps back, unable to redeem at a cost it will not bear, another Redeemer steps forward—one willing to bear the full cost in himself, to be 'impaired,' to be diminished, indeed to be made poor that we might be made rich. The nearer redeemer's 'I cannot' makes way for Boaz's 'I will'—and points beyond Boaz to the One who said, 'I lay down my life for the sheep.'

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sandal ceremony seals the transfer of the right of redemption. Boaz publicly declares before the elders and all the people that he has acquired the land and Ruth as his wife, to perpetuate the name of the dead. The people and elders pronounce a rich blessing, invoking Rachel, Leah, Tamar, and Perez, praying for fruitfulness and renown.
verseByVerse.theology: Boaz steps forward as the willing redeemer who bears the full cost gladly. The sandal ceremony (Deut 25:9) and the public declaration establish the redemption as legally complete and witnessed. The blessing of the people, invoking the matriarchs and the line of Perez (Judah's son by Tamar—another irregular union that advanced the messianic line), situates this redemption within the grand sweep of God's covenant purposes. Redemption here is public, costly, witnessed, and woven into the redemptive-historical line leading to David and the Messiah.
verseByVerse.examples: Boaz models the willing redeemer who counts the beloved worth every cost. Where the nearer kinsman calculated and withdrew, Boaz commits without reservation. The community's blessing reminds us that redemption and marriage are not merely private affairs but matters of covenant community, witnessed and celebrated by the people of God. The invocation of unlikely women in Israel's history (Tamar, and implicitly Rahab and Ruth) shows God's grace working through outsiders and irregular circumstances to accomplish his saving purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: Now this was the custom in former times in Israel concerning redeeming and exchanging: to confirm a transaction, the one drew off his sandal and gave it to the other, and this was the manner of attesting in Israel. So when the redeemer said to Boaz, "Buy it for yourself," he drew off his sandal. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The narrator pauses to explain an ancient custom for readers of a later generation—a sign that the book was written down some time after the events, when the practice had become unfamiliar. To confirm a legal transaction of redemption or exchange, "the one drew off his sandal and gave it to the other." The sandal ceremony served as a legally binding, publicly witnessed gesture of transfer—a kind of ancient signature or handshake that sealed the deal beyond dispute. The custom carries echoes of Deuteronomy 25:9, where in a refused levirate marriage the widow would remove the sandal of the unwilling kinsman as a sign of his shame; here the gesture is voluntary and dignified, simply a formal transfer of the right of redemption. "So when the redeemer said to Boaz, 'Buy it for yourself,' he drew off his sandal." With this simple act, the nearer kinsman relinquishes his claim, and the path is now clear for Boaz to redeem. Carson notes the narrator's care to establish the complete legality and propriety of the transaction—Ruth's redemption is no shadowy arrangement but a fully witnessed, formally sealed transfer in accordance with Israelite custom. The drawing off of the sandal is the visible, public moment when the law's prior claimant steps aside and the willing redeemer takes his place. The transaction that will lead to David, and to David's greater Son, is sealed with the humble removal of a shoe in a village gate.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Boaz said to the elders and all the people, "You are witnesses this day that I have bought from the hand of Naomi all that belonged to Elimelech and all that belonged to Chilion and to Mahlon. Also Ruth the Moabite, the widow of Mahlon, I have bought to be my wife, to perpetuate the name of the dead in his inheritance, that the name of the dead may not be cut off from among his brothers and from the gate of his native place. You are witnesses this day." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Boaz makes his great public declaration, and it rings with the joy of a redeemer who counts the cost worth paying. "You are witnesses this day"—he frames the whole community as legal witnesses to his act. He has bought all that belonged to Elimelech and his sons, and—the crown of his declaration—"Also Ruth the Moabite, the widow of Mahlon, I have bought to be my wife." Where the nearer kinsman recoiled at the cost, Boaz embraces it with open arms. And note his stated purpose: "to perpetuate the name of the dead in his inheritance, that the name of the dead may not be cut off." Boaz's redemption is profoundly self-giving—he acts not for his own gain but to preserve the name and line of a dead kinsman, to fill the emptiness of Naomi's house, to give Ruth a home. The narrator, for the final time, calls her "Ruth the Moabite"—the outsider made wife, the foreigner brought fully into the covenant, the alien now bound to the line that will produce the Messiah. Ferguson observes the gospel pattern shining here: the willing redeemer pays the full price to make the destitute his own, to give his name to one who had none, to raise up life where there was death. This is precisely what Christ has done—bought his bride at infinite cost, given her his name, perpetuated life where there was only the cutting off of death. "You are witnesses this day." And so are we, as we read—witnesses to a redemption that prefigures our own.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the people who were at the gate and the elders said, "We are witnesses. May the LORD make the woman, who is coming into your house, like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel. May you act worthily in Ephrathah and be renowned in Bethlehem, and may your house be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, because of the offspring that the LORD will give you by this young woman." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The community responds with a magnificent threefold blessing, rich with redemptive-historical resonance. First, they pray that Ruth might be "like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel"—the two wives of Jacob who, with their handmaids, bore the twelve tribes. To liken Ruth the Moabite to the great matriarchs of Israel is a stunning affirmation of her full inclusion; the foreigner is welcomed as a mother of the nation. Second, they bless Boaz with worthiness and renown in Ephrathah and Bethlehem. Third—and most remarkably—they invoke "the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah." This is a deliberate and astonishing reference. Tamar, like Ruth, was an outsider in an irregular situation, who through unusual means (Gen 38) secured offspring for the line of Judah and bore Perez—from whom Boaz himself descended. The people are recognizing that God has often advanced his covenant purposes through unlikely women and irregular circumstances. Wenham notes the genealogical foreshadowing: the mention of Perez points forward to the genealogy that will close the book and connect this story to David. The community cannot see how fully their blessing will be answered—"the offspring that the LORD will give you" will be Obed, then Jesse, then David, then, in the fullness of time, the Messiah. Three outsider women—Tamar, Rahab, Ruth—stand in the line of Christ (Matt 1:3–5), monuments to the grace of a God who delights to redeem the outsider and to write his glory through the unlikely.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — The Redeemer's Son and the Line of David
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Boaz marries Ruth, and the LORD gives her conception; she bears a son. The women bless Naomi, declaring the child a restorer of life and praising Ruth as worth more than seven sons. Naomi takes the child to her bosom, and the women name him Obed—the father of Jesse, the father of David.
verseByVerse.theology: The narrator attributes the conception directly to the LORD (v. 13)—after ten years of barrenness in Moab, God gives life. The God who emptied Naomi (1:21) now fills her arms. The child is called a 'restorer of life' and 'nourisher in old age'—the reversal of Naomi's emptiness is complete. And the closing genealogical note transforms the intimate story into a hinge of redemptive history: Obed, Jesse, David. The hidden providence of the whole book is revealed as the outworking of God's plan to bring forth the messianic king.
verseByVerse.examples: Naomi, who returned empty and bitter, now holds a grandchild to her bosom—the living proof that God's providence was for her all along. The women's praise of Ruth as 'more to you than seven sons' honors the foreign daughter-in-law above the highest cultural blessing. The story teaches that God fills the empty, restores the broken, and weaves the smallest faithful lives into the grandest purposes. No act of loyal love is wasted in the economy of God.

verseByVerse.quote: So Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife. And he went in to her, and the LORD gave her conception, and she bore a son. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: In a single verse the long-awaited redemption is consummated and crowned. "So Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife"—the worthy man and the worthy woman are joined; the redeemer has covered his bride; the threshing-floor pledge is fulfilled at last. But the most theologically significant phrase is what follows: "the LORD gave her conception." The narrator could have simply said Ruth conceived; instead he attributes the conception directly and emphatically to the LORD. This is profoundly important. Remember that Ruth had been married to Mahlon for some ten years in Moab without bearing a child (1:4–5); her barrenness, like that of Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, and Hannah, had seemed an insurmountable obstacle. Now God opens her womb and gives life. Sproul notes that the narrator's explicit ascription of the conception to the LORD is the theological capstone of the whole book: the God who seemed hidden throughout—who emptied Naomi, who worked behind the 'coincidences,' who never spoke directly in the narrative—is here named as the giver of life, the author of the redemption that has unfolded. The God who brought Naomi back empty (1:21) now fills her family with new life through a child the LORD himself has given. And this child, conceived by divine gift, will stand in the line that leads to David and to the Christ. Every human act in the story—Ruth's loyalty, Boaz's redemption—has been the instrument; but the life itself, the future itself, is the gift of God. The empty womb is filled by the hand of heaven.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the women said to Naomi, "Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a redeemer, and may his name be renowned in Israel! He shall be to you a restorer of life and a nourisher of your old age, for your daughter-in-law who loves you, who is more to you than seven sons, has given birth to him." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The women of Bethlehem, who in chapter 1 had asked in shock "Is this Naomi?" as she returned in bitterness, now gather to bless her in joy. And their words complete the great reversal of the book. "Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a redeemer"—the same God whom Naomi had accused of dealing bitterly with her is now praised as the One who has provided redemption. Interestingly, the "redeemer" the women refer to here is most immediately the child himself, who as heir will perpetuate the family line and secure Naomi's future—though the language also gathers up Boaz's redemptive act. The child "shall be to you a restorer of life and a nourisher of your old age." The woman who had nothing—no husband, no sons, no future—now has a grandchild who will sustain her, restore her, fill her empty years. And then comes one of the most beautiful tributes in all of Scripture: the women praise Ruth, Naomi's "daughter-in-law who loves you, who is more to you than seven sons." In a culture that prized sons above all, to say that a foreign daughter-in-law was worth more than seven sons (seven being the number of completeness) was the highest possible honor. Begg observes the stunning grace: the Moabite outsider, once labeled by her foreignness at every turn, is now celebrated as the supreme blessing of Naomi's life. The empty woman is full; the bitter woman is blessed; the God she accused has redeemed her beyond all her hopes. Hesed has triumphed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Naomi took the child and laid him on her lap and became his nurse. And the women of the neighborhood gave him a name, saying, "A son has been born to Naomi." They named him Obed. He was the father of Jesse, the father of David. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The image is almost unbearably tender: "Naomi took the child and laid him on her lap and became his nurse." The woman who cried "call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me," who declared "I went away full, and the LORD has brought me back empty"—now holds a child to her bosom. The empty arms are full at last. The women proclaim, "A son has been born to Naomi," recognizing that through Ruth's child the line of Elimelech, which had seemed utterly extinguished in the deaths of chapter 1, is restored and continued. The bitterness of chapter 1 is answered by the blessing of chapter 4; the emptiness is filled to overflowing. "They named him Obed," a name meaning "servant" or "worshiper." And then the narrator delivers the breathtaking genealogical climax that transforms this intimate village story into a hinge of cosmic redemptive history: "He was the father of Jesse, the father of David." David! The greatest king of Israel, the man after God's own heart, the recipient of the everlasting covenant promise (2 Sam 7), traces his ancestry through this very child—through Obed, through Boaz the redeemer, through Ruth the Moabite outsider. Carson notes that the genealogy is the narrator's way of revealing the true scope of the providence we have been watching: God was never merely arranging the comfort of two widows; he was forging a link in the chain that leads to the throne of David and beyond. The little story has become the great story. The barley field has led to the palace—and beyond the palace, to the manger.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — The Genealogy: From Perez to David
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book closes with a formal genealogy of ten generations, from Perez (son of Judah) to David. This list frames the entire story within the grand sweep of God's covenant purposes, revealing that the intimate account of Ruth and Boaz was a vital link in the line leading to Israel's great king—and, ultimately, to the Messiah.
verseByVerse.theology: The genealogy is the theological key that unlocks the book's ultimate purpose. The story of Ruth is not merely a beautiful tale of loyalty and redemption; it is part of the messianic line. The ten-generation list from Perez to David situates the redemption of a Moabite widow within the covenant promise to Judah (Gen 49:10) and the coming of the king. Matthew 1:5 will pick up this very line, placing Ruth in the genealogy of Jesus Christ. The hidden providence of the whole book is revealed as God's purpose to bring forth the Son of David, the King of kings.
verseByVerse.examples: The genealogy reminds us that God works across generations, weaving individual lives of faith into purposes that span centuries. Ruth and Boaz could not see that their loyal love would lead to David and to Christ; they simply acted faithfully in their moment. So we are called to faithfulness in our own small stories, trusting that God is weaving them into a tapestry whose full design we cannot yet see. The smallest acts of hesed echo into eternity.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these are the generations of Perez: Perez fathered Hezron, Hezron fathered Ram, Ram fathered Amminadab, Amminadab fathered Nahshon, Nahshon fathered Salmon, Salmon fathered Boaz, Boaz fathered Obed, Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The book closes not with the tender scene of Naomi and the child but with a formal, ten-name genealogy stretching from Perez to David—and this is no dry appendix but the theological crown of the whole work. "These are the generations of Perez"—the same Perez whom the people invoked in their blessing (4:12), the son of Judah by Tamar, another outsider through whom God advanced the messianic line. The list moves through ten generations, a structured and complete number, culminating in the resounding final name: "and Jesse fathered David." Everything in the book has been building toward this. The famine, the bereavements, the loyal vow on the road from Moab, the 'chance' arrival in Boaz's field, the bold request at the threshing floor, the willing redeemer at the gate, the child given by the LORD—all of it, the narrator now reveals, was God's hidden work to bring forth David, Israel's great king, the man after God's own heart, the recipient of the covenant promise of an everlasting throne (2 Sam 7:12–16). And the New Testament will carry the line one decisive step further: Matthew 1:5 places Ruth the Moabite explicitly in the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the Son of David, the King of kings. Keller's reflection is fitting: the tiny story of a destitute foreign widow and a worthy redeemer turns out to be a vital link in the chain that leads from the barley fields of Bethlehem to the manger of Bethlehem, from the gleaning of grain to the bread of life. The God of hidden providence, who seemed absent and silent through the suffering, was all along weaving redemption—not only for Naomi and Ruth, but for the world. Ruth the outsider, drawn under the wings of grace, becomes a mother of the Messiah. Grace all the way down, and grace all the way home.

4.theology:
The Willing Redeemer and the Law That Cannot Save. The contrast between the nearer kinsman and Boaz is the book's Christological climax. The nearer redeemer has the right and resources but lacks the willingness—'I cannot redeem it, lest I impair my own inheritance' (v. 6). He represents the law: it has a prior, legitimate claim on us as lawbreakers, but it cannot redeem, for to do so would compromise its righteous demands. Boaz steps forward as the willing redeemer who gladly bears the full cost: 'I will redeem her.' So Christ, the eternal Son with every right and infinite resources, was supremely willing to be 'impaired'—made poor, made sin, made a curse—that we might be redeemed. Redemption that costs nothing is no redemption at all.

The God Who Fills the Empty. The narrator's explicit statement that 'the LORD gave her conception' (v. 13) is the theological capstone of the book. The God who seemed hidden throughout—who emptied Naomi and never spoke directly—is revealed as the giver of life and the author of redemption. The woman who returned 'empty' (1:21) now holds a child to her bosom (v. 16); the bitter woman is blessed; the accused God is praised. This is Romans 8:28 in narrative form: God working all things, even the deaths and the emptiness, for the good of those who love him and are called according to his purpose.

Grace to the Outsider in the Line of the Messiah. Ruth the Moabite—labeled by her foreignness to the very end—stands in the genealogy that leads to David and, through Matthew 1:5, to Jesus Christ. Alongside Tamar and Rahab, she is a monument to the grace of a God who delights to redeem the outsider and to write his glory through the unlikely. The dividing wall between Jew and Gentile, which the cross would demolish (Eph 2:11–13), is already breached in a barley field, foreshadowing the gospel that will reach every nation.

Then: The transaction at the city gate reflects the legal customs of ancient Israel—the assembly of elders as witnesses, the law of land redemption (Lev 25:25) intertwined with levirate marriage (Deut 25:5–10), and the sandal ceremony that sealed the transfer. The community's role as witnesses and the public blessing show that redemption and marriage were matters of covenant community, not merely private arrangements. The invocation of Rachel, Leah, Tamar, and Perez situated the event within the grand story of God's dealings with Israel.

Now: Boaz confronts us with the question every redeemer faces: is the beloved worth the cost? Where the nearer kinsman calculated his own loss and withdrew, Boaz committed without reservation—a picture of the self-giving love that counts others worth every sacrifice. And the book's closing genealogy teaches us to live faithfully in our own small stories, trusting that God weaves them into purposes that span generations and reach into eternity. Naomi could not see, in her bitterness, that her empty arms would one day cradle the ancestor of the Messiah. So we are called to trust the God of hidden providence, who fills the empty, redeems the outsider, and brings forth—from the barley fields of our ordinary faithfulness—a glory we cannot yet imagine. Grace all the way down, and grace all the way home.
